The community kitchen on Alder Street smelled of scorched sugar and dish soap, and by six o'clock the industrial fans had pushed the heat of the afternoon out through the high windows, leaving behind a cool that reminded Madison of the boreal mornings she'd known at her grandmother's cabin, air so clean it seemed rinsed. She set her notebook on the steel counter beside a bag of couverture coins and read the note she'd copied from a food science page the night before: cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms. Six. She'd underlined it twice on the bus.

Her first two batches of homemade bars sat wrapped in wax paper at the far end of the counter, and she had brought them as evidence. Mr. Okafor, who ran the Tuesday night class, hadn't even needed to bite one. He'd snapped a corner, and instead of a clean break it had bent, then crumbled, and the surface was matte, streaked gray like an old car hood. "Untempered," he'd said, and left it at that, because the whole point of his teaching, he liked to say, was that you found things out with your hands.

Damaris had claimed the burner beside hers before Madison finished unpacking. Damaris was fifty-something, retired from the post office, and she wanted, she announced while chopping pistachios, to make her sister's sixtieth birthday bonbons, twelve of them, filled with apricot, because their mother used to make them at Easter and nobody in the family had since. "I don't care if they're ugly," she said, lining the little molds up like dominoes. "I care that they taste like 1987." She had already burned one bowl of chocolate and abandoned it to the sink with an apology.

The problem, as far as Madison could tell from her reading, was that all six crystal forms would happily set in cooling chocolate, but only one of them was worth having. Tempering aimed to make most of the cocoa butter set as form V, and form V was the one that gave shine and snap. The other five were the dull ones, the soft ones, the ones that bloomed white after a week. She'd drawn a little diagram in her margin, six boxes, the fifth starred, though she didn't actually know why the fifth was the good one, only that it was, and the not-knowing sat in her like a pebble.

She melted the coins in a steel bowl over water that was barely steaming, watching the thermometer as Mr. Okafor drifted past. "How does anyone get the same crystals twice?" she asked him. "If there are six, and they all want to form?"

"You seed it," he said, tapping the bag of coins. "A little unmelted chocolate carries the right crystals in. You spread them through." He was gone again before she could ask which crystals, so she worked it out herself, stirring chopped coins into the melted mass a few at a time, feeling the bowl warm against her palm, then cooler, then cooler.

Damaris leaned over to look at her thermometer. "You're treating it like chemistry class," she said. "I'd treat it like custard. You feel it on your wrist."

"It's both," Madison said, and meant it, and was a little surprised to hear herself say it, because at school she'd been made to feel that the two loyalties, the careful and the intuitive, were opposites. She kept stirring, slow figure eights, and thought the whole enterprise was a kind of symbiosis anyway, the seed crystals spreading through the warm mass, neither one much good alone. Though she could not have said whether the seeded crystals were form V or whether she was simply lucky, and she let that stay unresolved rather than pretend.

She poured a test strip onto the marble slab, let it set two minutes, and bent it. It snapped. Clean, with a sound like a knuckle, and the surface threw back the fluorescent light in one smooth sheet. "Form V," she said quietly, mostly to the chocolate. Damaris looked up from her apricot filling, and Madison held the shard out to her. "Six forms it can take. This is the one that shines."

Damaris took the piece, snapped it herself, and nodded slowly, the way people nod at evidence. "Then do mine next," she said, sliding her bowl across. "Twelve bonbons. 1987." Madison wiped the thermometer and reached for it.

The garage smelled of cut grass and old gasoline, and in the middle of it stood a keyboard on a folding table, its cord snaking to an outlet above the workbench. Camille had carried it out here in August because the house was full of her mother's boxes, half of them labeled for Goodwill and half labeled for the new apartment, and because her grandmother's piano, an upright too heavy to move, had been sold to a man who came with a dolly and two friends and a fistful of cash.

The keyboard was not the same. She had known it wouldn't be. What she hadn't expected was that she would miss the metronome more than the piano, the wooden pyramid with the brass pendulum that had sat on the piano's lid for as long as she could remember. When the buyers came, her grandmother had lifted it off before they touched a key, wrapped it in a dish towel, and set it in Camille's hands like something rescued from a fire.

"You keep that," her grandmother had said. "It belonged to your great-grandfather." That was all the provenance she offered. Now it sat on the workbench beside a coffee can of screws, and Camille, who had three weeks before she left for college and a beginner's book open to a page of Czerny exercises, slid the weight up the pendulum and set it ticking.

She had never once used it while her grandmother played. Grandmother played the way water moves downhill, without visible governance, and when eight-year-old Camille had asked who kept time for her, she had said, "I do, mostly," and laughed. But Camille's own time was not like that. Without the tick she rushed, and when she slowed herself deliberately she dragged, and both wrongnesses felt identical from the inside, which frightened her a little, that she could not hear her own errors.

She practiced an hour a day, sometimes two, because three weeks was nothing and she wanted, before she left, to get through the first book. Her mother thought she was hiding from the packing. "You could help me decide about the dining table," she said through the garage door one evening, and Camille said, "In a minute," and meant it and did not move, because her hands had just done something they had never done, played four measures with the left hand joining the right without a collapse.

That was the night she started wondering about the metronome itself. She looked it up on her phone between exercises: Johann Maelzel had patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, though the design drew on one by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel. She said it out loud to the empty garage, twice, because she wanted to be able to tell her grandmother she'd asked, that she'd wanted to know the way her grandmother had always wanted her to want to know things. There was a phone message already drafted to her, about the patent and about Winkel, about how strange it was that the machine dividing time so neatly had a contested origin at its heart.

She deleted the draft. Her grandmother was on a sabbatical of sorts, a year in Portugal that she'd announced in March with a postcard and no further explanation, and phone calls went to voicemail that filled and was never cleared. Camille had tried twice in July and then stopped, partly out of pride, mostly because she suspected the silence was a kind of delimiting, a line drawn around what her grandmother would and would not carry with her across the ocean, and the metronome, apparently, was on the far side of it, given away along with everything else.

Except that wasn't tenable either, because the woman who wrapped a hundred-year-old instrument in a dish towel and pressed it into her granddaughter's hands was not simply cutting herself off. Camille played through the Czerny again, slower than the book asked, the pendulum ticking beside her like a patient second mind. Maybe the machine was the message instead of the abandonment. Maybe her grandmother had given her the one object she owned that said: time can be held, measured, kept, even by a person who claims to keep it herself.

She could hold both ideas now, the gift and the leaving, without deciding between them, and that felt more honest than choosing, though it settled nothing. The last evening before the drive to campus, she carried the metronome to the keyboard, set the weight where she'd learned it belonged, and played the final exercise in the book clean through, both hands, at sixty beats to the minute. The pendulum swung, brass catching the light of the bare bulb. When the last chord faded she let the ticking run on by itself for a while, and then she stopped it with one finger.

Brandon spread the flashcards across the picnic table in the backyard, weighting the corners with rocks because the August wind kept trying to take them. Glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain: four stacks, shuffled out of order, and somewhere among them the mistake that had cost him eleven points on the last exam. In two weeks he would be a college student, the first from his family, and the biology placement test was the last gate between him and the fall.

Nadia came out through the screen door with two glasses of lemonade and the particular patience of someone who had already finished her own placement tests. "Still the mitochondria thing?"

"It's not a thing, it's a process." He picked up a card, turned it over, put it down. "I can recite it. Glucose gets broken down, eventually you get ATP. But reciting isn't knowing, and I can't tell the difference anymore."

"So don't recite. Tell me like I'm five."

He tried, and the words went stale in his mouth. Carriers, protons, a gradient across a membrane. Nadia squinted at the fence instead of at him, and he understood that he had lost her, which meant he had lost the thread himself.

Then he remembered the science museum, the spring of sophomore year, the field trip he had almost skipped to go to a concert. He had wandered off from the group and stood alone in a dim hall where a model turned inside a glass case. It was a lumpy sphere with a stalk, like a mushroom, and the stalk spun, quietly, endlessly, protons pouring through it and the head rotating with the motion, and a placard had said that the turning built the fuel of the cell. He had watched it for ten minutes because it was hypnotic and because it was the first time the diagrams in his textbook had ever moved. He hadn't connected it to anything. He had gone home and forgotten it for two years.

"It was ATP synthase," he said now, standing up so fast the cards scattered. "There's an enzyme, ATP synthase, and it works like a tiny rotary motor. Protons flow through it and that makes part of the enzyme spin, and the spinning builds the ATP. That's the step I've been missing. The whole chain before it, all those proton pumps, they're just loading the spring. Then the motor turns." He grabbed a stick off the ground and drew a mushroom shape in the dirt beside the table, arrowed protons through the stalk, twisted his wrist to show the head rotating.

Nadia leaned over the drawing, then over the cards, matching his stick figure to the tidy printed diagram. "So the test question you missed."

"I said the protons make ATP directly. I dichotomized it wrong, is what I did. I split it into either chemistry or machinery, like I had to pick one lens, and it's both at once. It's a chemical gradient running a mechanical motor." He heard himself and wondered if that sounded like insight or like showing off, and let the judgment sit unresolved. Some discernment he had earned honestly, from getting it wrong first. Some of it was still extrinsic, borrowed from the museum placard and repeated without ownership, and he could not yet tell which parts were which.

They sat with the lemonade while the wind kept picking at the cards. Nadia asked whether the same thing was happening in her, right now, in the muscles of her arm holding the glass, and Brandon said probably, constantly, in every cell of the grass and the fence and the wasp investigating the spilled sugar on the table. Motors turning by the trillion in a backyard on an ordinary afternoon.

Then she turned over the last card, the one he had been avoiding, and read it aloud, and the answer printed on the back was not the answer he had just given her. His version and the textbook's version disagreed about where the protons came from, and one of them was wrong, and for a moment he could not decide which. He looked at the stick figure in the dirt, already beginning to blur at the edges.

"Call the museum," Nadia said.

Sarah spread the ocean current map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with a horseshoe, a watering can, and her brother's left shoe, which he had sacrificed to science with ceremonial gravity. The assignment was due Monday: explain, in one page, how the Gulf Stream keeps northern Europe warmer than it had any right to be. Her laptop sat closed beside her because she had decided, in a fit of ambition, to figure it out from the paper map first, the way her grandmother had once figured out bus routes from folded schedules, holding the whole system in her head.

Her friend Priya arrived over the fence, as she always did, holding a popsicle like a scepter. "You're doing homework in the yard," Priya said. "Voluntarily. On a Saturday. Should I call someone?"

"You could be the someone," Sarah said. "Look at this. The arrows."

Priya leaned over the map, orange syrup dripping dangerously close to Iceland. The Atlantic was webbed with arrows, fat red ones and thinner blue ones, crossing and curving like a diagram of a very organized flock of birds. Priya stabbed her popsicle stick at a red arrow off the coast of Florida. "That one's going fast. That's why it's red, right? Red means fast. Like, warning, this water is speeding."

Sarah frowned. It was a reasonable guess, and something about it bothered her precisely because it was reasonable. She traced the red arrows north along the American coast, then watched them swing east across the Atlantic toward Europe, and then, when they arrived, they seemed to fade, or the mapmakers had simply stopped drawing them with the same conviction. "But look," she said. "There's a blue arrow going down this coast, and it's the same thickness as the red one going up. If thickness meant speed, wouldn't they be different?" Priya licked her popsicle and offered no verdict, which was her way of saying she was now there for the popsicle and the company.

Sarah sat back on the bench and stared at the sky as though it might contain a footnote. Warm and cold. Red and blue. Her little brother, Marcus, ambushed a ladybug on the fence, and she almost called out to ask him to stop, except a thought arrived with such force that she forgot the ladybug entirely. Red meant warm. Blue meant cold. It was the same code as every faucet she had ever used and every weather map Priya's dour grandfather watched with the volume too loud. The arrows weren't showing speed at all; they were showing temperature. She had been reading the map wrong for twenty minutes, and Marcus had been reading faucets right his whole life.

"On this map," she said slowly, testing it, "warm currents are the red arrows. Cold ones are the blue arrows." Priya squinted, then pointed at a blue arrow crawling down the east side of the Atlantic. "So that's cold water heading south. And the red one going north past Florida is warm water." Sarah nodded, feeling the whole map rearrange itself in her head, like furniture being moved in a dark room and suddenly the lamp found.

The Gulf Stream was the fat red ribbon, warm water pouring north, carrying heat the way a delivery truck carries pizzas, and Europe sat at the end of its route. That was the page she had to write. But a second problem had surfaced, sneakier than the first: her teacher's rubric wanted "a considered position," which Sarah suspected was code for admitting you didn't know everything without sounding like you knew nothing.

She went inside for lemonade and came back to find Marcus holding her phone, reading with the expression of a tiny dissident reviewing government paperwork. "You got a message," he announced. "From a person named Mom. It says, and I quote, 'Grandma wants to know if you've figured out the ocean thing yet. She says when she was a girl the maps were all in one color and you had to read the words.'" Sarah took the phone. There was more, in her grandmother's style, appended like a postscript from another century: "Tell Sarah the ocean does not care what color we paint it."

Priya found this hilarious for reasons she could not articulate, and Marcus began narrating the map as though it were a nature documentary, giving the currents voices. The red arrows spoke in a warm, slightly smug tone about their vacation plans in Norway; the blue arrows muttered about the poles and complained that nobody ever wrote songs about them. Sarah laughed, then stopped laughing, because the joke had snagged on something true. The colors were a choice. Grandma's maps had one color and words; Sarah's had colors and no words; both were right, and both were someone's decision about what a reader would understand fastest. Priya had guessed speed because speed mattered to her, the fastest way over the fence, the fastest popsicle consumption in the western suburbs.

By late afternoon Sarah had a draft, a sunburn on one shoulder, and a page that said the Gulf Stream carried warm water north and east across the Atlantic, warming the lands it passed, and that the red arrows on her map marked that warmth while the blue arrows marked cold water flowing the other way. She had also written a paragraph admitting that she'd first misread the colors, and that a map, like a grandmother, tells you what it chooses to tell you in the way it chooses to tell it. Priya read over her shoulder and pronounced it "weirdly good." Marcus demanded a speaking role in the final draft.

Sarah looked once more at the map before the wind could claim it. The red ribbon crossed the whole ocean, patient and unconcerned, doing exactly what it had done long before anyone drew it, and she weighted the European corner with the other shoe.

The community art studio closed at six, and Jordan's critique of Kahlo's "Self-Portrait on the Borderline between Mexico and the United States" was due, fully written, by seven, which meant he had roughly three hours to say something intelligent about a painting he had so far described in his notebook as "sad lady, plants, flag." His friend Priya had claimed the table by the window and was already highlighting her own reproduction with the focus of someone defusing a bomb.

"You've written two sentences," she said, without looking up.

"I've written a title and a strategy."

"Read me the strategy."

"It's more of a feeling."

Priya extended her hand. Jordan slid the notebook across and watched her face perform a small weather system, ending in rain. He grinned despite himself, because the truth was he had no strategy, and the summer program's instructor, Ms. Okafor, had promised that this critique would determine who got the studio's fall apprenticeship. Jordan wanted that apprenticeship the way you want something you haven't admitted to anyone: loudly, privately, and with a plan to deny it if asked.

He leaned over the reproduction. On the left, Mexico's side, lush greenery and ancient idols; on the right, the American side, machines and smoke; and Kahlo in the middle in a pink dress, holding a small Mexican flag. He'd started writing about the symbolism, the divided world, but it kept coming out like a book report, an apportionment of meaning, a little for Mexico, a little for the USA, a crumb for the dress. Then Priya made an irritated noise and pointed at the border where a red flower sat against all that green.

"Why does this look like it's plugged in?" she said. "The red here. It's practically humming."

Jordan squinted. She was right; the flower seemed to vibrate against the leaves behind it, a heat shimmer made of paint. He pulled the colour wheel poster off the wall and spun it around on the table, tracing from red across to green with one finger. Opposite each other, exactly.

"They're complementary colours," he said. "Red and green sit opposite each other on the wheel, and side by side, they make each other look brighter."

"Show off."

"I just found it. Look." He held the poster beside the painting. "It's not just that the flower is red. It's red against green, on purpose. She put the brightest thing on the Mexican side."

Priya, who could never let him aggrandize himself for more than four seconds, said, "Or it's just a flower, and nature likes red flowers, and you're building a cathedral out of a geranium." But she was already flipping to her notes on composition, drawing arrows with her pencil: the greenery arching upward on the left, the smokestacks descending on the right, the figure at the exact center, the sun and moon split above her. Jordan saw it at the same moment she did, the painting balanced like a scale, and the vibrating red flower tipping the whole thing toward Mexico.

"Two different readings, then," Priya said, tapping the table. "The composition says the sides are equal, perfectly mirrored. But the colour says the Mexican side is alive and the other side is dead. So which one wins?"

Jordan had been hoping she wouldn't ask that. He wrote, crossed out, wrote again. The studio's torpid afternoon heat was thickening into evening, and the guy at the front desk started stacking chairs at five-fifteen, a slow metallic announcement that time was running out. Jordan wrote about the composition's symmetry, then the complementary red and green breaking it, then a paragraph saying that Kahlo might intend both at once, that the painting could be balanced and biased simultaneously, and that he wasn't sure which claim to stake. It felt like a weakness in the essay. It also felt like the most honest sentence in it.

At five to six he hit print on the studio's ancient machine, which groaned, considered, and produced his pages still warm. Priya collected hers with two minutes to spare. Outside on the curb, waiting for his bus, Jordan read his last paragraph over her shoulder, out loud, and she said, "You hedged at the end."

"I reported a finding. The finding is that I can't tell."

"Ms. Okafor's going to say you need a stronger thesis."

"Ms. Okafor's going to say a lot of things." He folded the pages in half and put them in his backpack, careful of the warm ink. The bus turned the corner with its lights already on, and Priya nudged him with her elbow and said, "Cathedral of geraniums. I'm putting that on a mug."

The ballistics exhibit on the second floor had a launcher, a lever for speed, a dial for angle, and a foam pit divided into colored zones worth points, and Hayden had lost four dollars' worth of tokens missing every one of them. The launcher hissed, the rubber ball arced over the pit, and it dropped a full zone short of the hundred-point circle, the way it had dropped short all afternoon. Behind him a voice said, "You're aiming like the ball remembers where it was pointed." He turned and found a girl in a museum volunteer shirt, maybe his own age, restocking the token machine with the particular boredom of someone who had watched this exhibit for an entire summer.

"I'm aiming at the target," Hayden said.

"You're aiming at the target," she agreed, "but the ball isn't thinking about the target. It's doing two jobs at once." She pointed at the angle dial. "You've got one number controlling two things that don't talk to each other. The up part and the across part." Then she caught herself, the way people did when they'd been told not to coach the guests, and said she'd already said too much, and went back to her tokens.

He stood there with two tokens in his fist and felt a visceral refusal to spend them on another guess. Guessing had gotten him nothing. So he sat down on the bench beside the exhibit and did what he actually knew how to do, which was not physics but arguments: he'd spent the spring on the debate team, learning to split a claim into parts that could be examined separately. Split it, his coach said, and the thing either holds or it doesn't. Maybe a ball in the air was the same kind of problem. The upward motion was one claim, the sideways motion another, and the angle dial just stirred them together.

He watched three other visitors shoot. He timed them on his phone, interpolating between the two marks on his stopwatch screen when the ball crossed the flag near the top of its arc, because the timer only refreshed every tenth of a second and he wanted something finer than that. Higher shots stayed up longer. That made sense on its own terms. And then, watching a kid in a green jersey launch flat and low, he noticed the other half: the flat shots crossed the pit fast, and the steep ones drifted across slowly. So the speed of the ball and the angle carved the motion into a vertical piece and a horizontal piece, and each piece could be known separately.

He got out his notebook. If he timed how long a ball stayed in the air, and he knew how fast it was moving sideways, then the distance it covered across the pit would just be that constant sideways speed multiplied by the time it was up there. He wrote it as a single line, multiplied, and looked at the number. If the ball flew sideways at six meters per second and hung in the air for one second, it would land six meters out. Nothing in that sentence cared about the arc at all. The arc was just what the two separate motions looked like when you watched them together, a shape that came from adding, not a cause of anything.

The problem, when he pressed his pen against it, was the sideways speed itself. The lever gave him a setting, not a number, and the museum had never printed what the settings meant. Here his habits from debate offered nothing; an argument could be won by definition and rhetoric, by a well-built logos, but a ball landing two zones short didn't care how well he framed it. He would have to measure. He watched the kid in the green jersey fire again, counted his steps along the marked floor from launcher to landing point, timed the flight, and divided. One launch gave a rough answer. A second, at the same setting, gave a closer one. It was like the stopwatch: he was finding the true value by building in from both sides of it.

On his last token he set the angle low, waited for the hiss, and the ball crossed the whole pit in a flat, fast line and struck the back wall of the hundred-point circle with a sound like a knuckle on a door. The girl looked up from the token machine. He showed her the notebook, the one line of multiplication, and she read it and then laughed, one short syllable, and said, "You know the settings change every shot, right? It randomizes the speed. You just got lucky."

Hayden stood very still, holding the notebook open, because she was probably right, and because the ball had still landed exactly where his line had said it would, six meters out, and he could not make those two facts into one clean position yet. He closed the notebook slowly. "Then I'll measure again," he said, and held out his hand for another token.

The kitchen scale read 233.76 grams, and Mia had no idea what that meant, which was the problem. Her science fair project compared how salt affected the freezing point of water, and the rubric, which she had read four times at the table while the kettle heated, required her to report concentrations in moles, not grams. She had a bag of table salt, a borrowed scale from the chemistry room, and a Tuesday afternoon.

"Do you actually need the whole bag?" her brother Danny asked from the doorway. He was home for the weekend, which meant he was home to argue with their mother about loans. "Because some of us are trying to cook."

"I need all of it," Mia said, though she didn't. She needed to know how to convert, and the conversion was the thing no one had taught her yet. Mr. Reyes had covered it in a unit she'd missed during the flu week, and when she'd asked him after class he'd said, "It's all on the handout," which it was, in the sense that the words were on the page.

In the living room the television muttered about an outbreak of something in three counties, an epidemiology team being sent in, and their mother turned it up. Mia pulled the handout toward her across the counter. The numbers were all there. Sodium chloride, 58.44 grams per mole. She copied it onto the back of an envelope and then sat looking at it, because knowing the number was not the same as knowing what to do with it.

Danny came in and started chopping an onion two feet away from her papers. "Move the project."

"You move."

He didn't move, but he did glance at her envelope. "Is that the salt thing? People used to ask me that in tutoring. Kids fail that question constantly." He went back to the onion, and Mia waited, but he was not going to explain it, because Danny never explained anything; he hinted at it from a slight elevation and waited for you to climb up after him.

She looked at the bag. The label said the bag contained one kilogram, but she'd weighed out what she needed for the first trial and gotten 233.76 grams, a number she had chosen on purpose, because it looked divisible. She divided it by 58.44 and got four. Four exactly. She checked it twice, moving the pencil down the long division, and it came out four both times, and something in her chest went quiet, the way it did when a shot went in at practice.

"Four moles," she said out loud.

"See," Danny said, "you didn't need me." He scraped the onion into the pan. From the living room their mother said something about how the districts would have to spread the cost over years, amortize it, or the budget would never survive, and Danny said that was exactly his point about the loans, and the two of them began their tectonic argument, the slow grinding one that moved an inch an hour and never produced a winner. Mia let it happen around her. She was writing the calculation into her lab notebook, units and all, so that when the judge asked her at the fair she could show the steps instead of mumbling.

Then she stopped. Because the four was suspicious. She had chosen 233.76 grams because she wanted a clean answer, which meant she had engineered the problem rather than solved it. The bag itself held about a kilogram, and a kilogram divided by 58.44 would not come out clean. She ran it anyway, roughly, and got a little over seventeen, some endless decimal she would have to round and justify rounding. She wrote both numbers down, the clean one and the messy one, and understood that the clean one was practice and the messy one was the actual world, and that from now on she would have to tell the difference herself, every time, because nobody was going to mark which was which.

"I'm going to need more salt," she said. "For the second trial."

"There's a bag in the pantry," Danny said, not turning from the stove. "But you have to tell me what a mole is first."

"It's the amount you get," Mia said, "when you divide the grams by the grams per mole." She stood up and opened the pantry door.

The Rileys' basement smelled like salsa and carpet cleaner, and by the second half of the final everyone had stopped pretending to sit. Zoe stood near the snack table with a paper plate she'd abandoned, watching France and Croatia fight through a match that kept bending toward something nobody could name yet. Her neighbor's husband, Mr. Riley, had invited half the block, and somewhere in the crush of them was her grandfather, who had driven four hours that morning just to watch the game with other people.

The problem was the bet. Or not the bet exactly, but her cousin Marcus, who had spent the whole tournament explaining football to her as though she hadn't played it for nine years. He'd bet her twenty dollars that Croatia would equalize before full time, and he'd spent the last ten minutes narrating why it was inevitable, his voice getting more incisive with every sentence, slicing through her patience. Four-two was the score. France ahead. Marcus insisted the game wasn't over.

"It's over when I have your twenty," Zoe said, and he grinned at her across the room, holding up a folded bill like a man at an auction.

Then Croatia scored. Or seemed to. The ball came off a scramble in the box and a forward toe-poked it in past the keeper with three minutes left, and the basement erupted into a wall of noise, half grief and half joy, and Zoe watched her twenty dollars die in Marcus's raised fist. He was already crossing the room toward her when the referee stopped, touched his ear, and drew a small rectangle in the air.

Nobody in the basement knew what it meant at first. Mr. Riley kept saying, "What is that, what is he doing," and someone's phone flashlight swung uselessly around the ceiling. It was Zoe who pulled out her own phone and searched, because if she was going to lose twenty dollars she wanted to know the mechanism of her losing. She read the screen twice before she said anything.

"They're checking it," she said, loud enough that the room turned. "It's the video assistant referee. This is the first World Cup to use it, in Russia. They can review goals, penalties, direct red cards, and cases of mistaken identity." Someone near the couch groaned the word VAR like it was a curse in a language he was just learning. Zoe's grandfather caught her eye across the room and lifted his chin, almost imperceptibly, the way he did when he was pleased and didn't want anyone to know.

The wait was strange. For a full minute the game simply stopped existing, and forty people stood in a basement watching men on a screen stand around a field watching nothing. Marcus came and leaned on the snack table beside her. "It'll count," he said. "It counted. Everyone saw it count."

"Then why are they still checking?"

He didn't answer, and in his silence she found herself remembering something she hadn't thought about in years: a game when she was eleven, a linesman's flag that had wrongly wiped out her goal in a tournament semifinal, her coach shouting, her father saying afterward that the injustice was part of the sport, that you had to take the bad calls with the good ones because that was the deal. She had believed him for a long time. She wasn't sure she believed him now. Standing there, she could hold both ideas at once, the old romance of human error and this new cold accuracy, and she couldn't make either one win. Maybe the pause was the price of getting it right. Maybe the pause was its own kind of wrong. She genuinely did not know.

The referee walked to the side of the field and looked at a screen, and the basement went so quiet that Zoe could hear the refrigerator in the next room. Then the referee raised his arm and crossed it, sharp and final, and the goal was gone. Disallowed. Croatia's reprieve, the one that would have sent the game spiraling into its last desperate minutes, was erased by a camera nobody in this basement would ever see. Marcus put both hands on the table and dropped his head.

Zoe held out her palm. "Twenty dollars."

He slapped the bill into it without looking up, and the room around them began gathering cups and jackets, the match bleeding out toward its whistle. It was her grandfather who spoke next, coming over with his coat already on. "You know," he said, taking a tortilla chip from her abandoned plate, "in my day the ref just guessed, and we lionized him anyway. Built him a little statue in our heads." He crunched the chip. "Terrible calls, every summer. We loved him for it."

Zoe folded the twenty into her pocket, and Marcus finally straightened up, held out his own phone, and said, "Double or nothing. France scores again before the whistle."

She looked at the clock. Ninety seconds, maybe, plus stoppage. She thought of the camera in its invisible room, patiently knowing everything.

"Done," she said, and shook his hand, just as the screen flashed a VAR box around a French striker standing alone, very still, half a field from the ball.

Brayden had agreed to his grandmother's book club the way you agree to things at a lake house in July, because the alternative was another afternoon of watching wasps investigate the railing. The club met on her screened porch, five women and one man named Gerald, all of them old enough to have opinions they considered final. They had chosen The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, and Brayden had read it in two sittings on the dock, annotating with a pencil he kept losing in the cushions of the Adirondack chair.

The problem surfaced immediately. "Nick is the moral center," said Gerald, tapping the table. "He tells us so himself. He says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.'" Around the porch, heads nodded, ice shifted in glasses, and Brayden felt the inchoate beginnings of an objection, something he couldn't yet put a shape to. He remembered Nick withholding things. He remembered feeling, at certain passages, that he was being handled.

"Except," he said, and then stopped, because everyone looked at him. "Except he doesn't tell Jordan he's from the Midwest when she asks, exactly. And he doesn't tell Daisy he knows about the affair, and he doesn't tell Tom about Myrtle, and he waits until it's convenient to say anything at all." His grandmother raised an eyebrow and poured him more lemonade, which he took as either encouragement or a disincentive, he couldn't tell which.

"That's discretion, dear," said a woman in a sunhat. "Not dishonesty." Brayden turned his glass in his hands. Was there a difference? He tried to work it out aloud. "Maybe the lying isn't the interesting part," he said slowly. "Maybe it's the claiming. He says he's honest right before he starts judging everybody, like the claim gives him permission." The porch went quiet in a way that felt productive rather than awkward.

Gerald leaned forward. "The author is using the narrator against us." Brayden had been circling that idea all week without naming it, and hearing it out loud sutured something together in his mind, the dock notes, the pencil, the sense of being handled. It wasn't that Nick lied constantly. It was that the whole book arrived filtered through a man who thought very well of himself, and you had to decide, sentence by sentence, how much to trust the filter. "So every scene is two stories," Brayden said. "What happened, and Nick's version of what happened. And we only get one of them."

His grandmother, who had been silent through all of this, set down her glass. "When I was your age, I believed him completely," she said. "Reread it at forty and thought, well, he knew exactly what he was doing with that girl in the yellow car and he drove home and ate dinner." Brayden laughed. That was the thing he hadn't expected: that the same sentences could change on you over decades, that trust in a narrator might be something you re-negotiate your whole life.

He walked to the screen door and looked at the water, trying to hold both ideas at once. Maybe Nick was honest compared to the people around him, which is a low bar in a novel full of carelessness and money. Maybe he was honest about small things and dishonest about the shape of the story he was telling. Brayden couldn't resolve it, and it occurred to him that the irresolution might be the point, that Fitzgerald had built a machine you couldn't finish assembling.

They passed around a plate of peach slices while Gerald argued that the green light proved his theory and the sunhat woman argued it proved hers. Brayden took a slice and flipped back through his pages, finding the pencil marks, the underlined claim, the margins full of questions he'd written to no one. On the last page he found one he didn't remember making: "Do I do this too?" He showed it to his grandmother. She read it, and laughed, and put her hand briefly on his shoulder. "Read it again in thirty years," she said, "and tell me the answer."

Colton had promised himself he would finish Wuthering Heights before Monday, and by Sunday night he had read all of it in one greedy, resentful sitting, the desk lamp burning past one in the morning while his mother knocked twice on the door. He arrived at English with the paperback soft from his grip and a feeling he could not yet name: that he had been told the story by someone, not shown it, and that the someone had opinions.

Ms. Okafor had taped a question to the board: Who is speaking, and what do they want? It looked simple. It was not, and Colton suspected she knew that, because she sat on the edge of her desk and said almost nothing for the first ten minutes.

Priya raised her hand first. She said she'd been rereading the middle chapters and had started wondering about Nelly. "She doesn't like some of these people," Priya said. "And she's the one telling us everything about them. Does that change what we're allowed to believe?" A few people laughed, the way people laugh when a question loosens something. Colton didn't laugh. He flipped back to the opening chapters, where Lockwood, this nervous visitor, sits by the fire and gets the whole history out of the housekeeper over several evenings, and realized he had been reading it exactly that way the whole time without seeing the frame. Two people stood between him and every event. Two sets of hands.

The class argued. Damon thought Nelly was basically honest, just sharp-tongued, and that the novel needed a servant's view because the gentry would never have told the truth about themselves. Marcus countered that Nelly interferes constantly, she's in the middle of everything, carrying messages, keeping secrets, and then she gets to decide how it all sounds. "She's not a window," Marcus said. "She's a filter."

Colton had written nothing down. He kept thinking about a thing from the summer, which was that he had told his cousin the story of his breakup with Dana, told it well, with timing and a devastating closing line, and his cousin had taken his side completely, and it had felt like winning. It was only in September, when Dana said flatly, "That's not how it went, and you know it," that he understood a narrator can be sincere and self-serving in the same breath. He had abrogate on the tip of his mind, some half-remembered vocabulary word, and dismissed it; what he meant was simpler. Telling a story is a kind of power, and he had used it.

He raised his hand, which he rarely did. "Everything we know about Heathcliff comes through Nelly to Lockwood," he said. "So when she calls him a fiend, that's not the novel calling him a fiend. That's her. And Lockwood writes it all down, and he's not exactly a genius either. He misreads everyone in his own scenes." Ms. Okafor asked whether that meant the book had no center. Colton said he didn't think so. "I think the center is the gap. What we can't get to, because two people are standing in the doorway."

Priya turned around in her seat. "So do we trust her or not?"

He wanted to say not. It would have been clean, an answer with edges. But he kept seeing the summer again, himself at the kitchen table with his cousin, both of them certain, and Dana later at her locker, absolutely certain too, and himself no longer able to say which version he had falsified on purpose and which he had only wanted. "I trust her the way I'd trust a person," he said. "Partly. She's in the story she's telling. She hates people and loves people and she was there for all of it, and being there isn't the same as seeing it straight." He could hear how inchoate it sounded, the idea arriving before the words for it, and he kept going anyway. "The question isn't reliable or unreliable. It's what she wanted while she talked, and I don't think we fully get that."

Damon said that was a cop-out, that a narrator either deserves trust or doesn't, and Colton felt the old pull toward a verdict, the relief of one. He also felt that the characters had gotten more real to him in the last forty minutes than in the whole night of reading, as if they'd only now acquired sentience, because now they were being told by someone, and everyone who tells is partial. Both things were true and they didn't sit together easily.

Ms. Okafor took the question off the board and wrote a new one underneath: If you retold this novel, what would you keep out? She said the essays were due Friday, then walked to the window and opened it, as though the room had gotten heavy. Colton looked at his paperback, its cracked spine, Nelly's voice still running in his head like a faucet someone had left on. He turned to the back inside cover and wrote his name under Dana's, where he'd written it back in June, when he'd lent her the book and thought he knew how everything would go.

Noah's first real paycheque arrived on a Friday folded inside an envelope with the schedule for next week, and he waited until the bus home to open it, the way you wait to bite into something you suspect will disappoint you. He had done the arithmetic in his head all through his shift at the harbour restaurant: eleven dollars an hour, thirty-one hours, trays carried, ketchup refilled, three Saturdays of a boy named Ruari covering for his shift manager's moods. The number he had expected was three hundred and forty-one dollars. The number on the cheque was two hundred and eighty-six.

He counted it twice, as though the paper might rearrange itself. Behind the counter at home his mother was slicing peppers, and he asked her, keeping his voice flat, whether the restaurant could just take money off a cheque like that. She shrugged toward the drawer where the filing lived and said it was probably taxes, probably normal, and the word probably sat in him like a seed of doubt all evening.

The next night a family from Leeds came in for the early seating, ordered fish and chips and sticky toffee pudding, and left their itemized receipt behind on the table when they went. Noah bussed the plates, then paused. He was saving receipts lately, every one, because he and his friend Devi had started comparing prices against a list she kept from her cousin in Manchester. He slid the British receipt into his apron pocket and finished the table without looking at it again, because Ruari was watching, and Ruari had opinions about slowness.

At Devi's kitchen table on Sunday, the two receipts lay side by side, his own from a Canadian grocery run and the one from the restaurant, and Devi tapped the Canadian one. "See, here, at the bottom, after the subtotal. HST, thirteen percent, added on at the till. Your ninety-dollar shop is really a hundred and one seventy." She tapped the Leeds one. "This one just ends. No tax line at all." Noah frowned and turned the paper over, as though the missing amount might be hiding on the back. Devi was already typing, her laptop fan whirring. "It's called VAT," she said, reading. "Value added tax. It's built into the prices there, so it doesn't show up as a separate line." She scrolled. "Okay, so it's been twenty percent over there since January fourth, twenty eleven." Noah leaned in to see the date himself, printed on the page, because Devi had been confidently wrong before, once, about the boiling point of sugar syrup, and they had argued about it for a week.

"So the pudding," he said slowly, "already had its tax inside the price." He thought of the family from Leeds leaving what they owed, exact, no surprises at the end, while his own receipt had grown a tail at the register. It felt like two different theories of honesty, one that showed you the cost upfront and one that added it at the last second and called it the same meal.

That was when he remembered the other paper, still in his jacket, and pulled out his pay stub, the thin sheet that had come with the cheque and that he had folded away without reading. Devi took it and went quiet in a way that made his stomach tighten. The kitchen clock ticked. She ran her finger down the columns, and he watched her face for the verdict before he would look himself. "Here," she said finally, and turned it toward him. Income tax. CPP. Employment insurance. Each with its own small, lawful bite taken out of the three forty-one before it ever reached him.

He had been prepared, on the walk over, to march into the restaurant on Monday and accuse Ruari of skimming, and he had rehearsed the sentence, and now the sentence dissolved on his tongue. It was strange to feel relieved and annoyed at once, to get less than he wanted and still have nothing to fight. He tried to say something wise about it and Devi cut him off. "Don't expatiate," she said. "You sound like my uncle at Christmas." He laughed, and then he said, "Okay, but is it the same thing, though? The tax on my wages and the tax on the pudding?" She considered it, spinning a bottle cap on the table. "Semantics," she said, "whether you call it a deduction or a price. Either way you pay it." He said he didn't think it was only semantics, that seeing the number felt different from not seeing it, and she said maybe, and let the cap spin down flat.

On Monday he arrived early, before the dinner rush, and asked Ruari for extra shifts anyway, because the laptop was still three hundred and forty dollars away and the arithmetic was the arithmetic. He also kept the Leeds receipt, flattened it, and put it in the folder with his pay stub, the two of them side by side like specimens of the same animal caught in different countries. Ruari handed him a tray and pointed at table six, where a couple had just sat down and were still holding their menus up in front of their faces.

Kaitlyn had mixed the gray herself, working from a tube of black and a tube of white with a whisper of blue, and for the first hour she had been proud of it. The gray was for the lake in her painting, the lake at the bottom of the hill where the whole camp swam every afternoon, and she wanted it to look the way it looked at seven in the morning, before anyone had touched the water. But when she set the canvas on the easel and stepped back, the lake looked wrong in a way she couldn't name. On the left side, where she had painted the orange tents of the boys' unit, the gray seemed warm, almost brown. On the right side, beside a band of blue-green that was supposed to be the pines, the same gray looked cold, almost lavender, as though she had used two different mixtures. She checked the palette. It was one gray. She had used one gray.

The art show was tomorrow night. Parents drove up the gravel road at six, and everything had to be dry and hung by five, and the counselor Ruby had made it clear that she would not be staying up until midnight with anyone who wasted the afternoon. Kaitlyn had wasted the morning already, standing in front of the canvas in the craft barn, where the light came through the screen doors in long dusty panels and the smell of turpentine sat under everything.

Mira was at the next easel, painting a dragonfly with a magnifying glass beside her so she could count wing cells. Mira was fifteen and had arrived with a suitcase of library books, which she read while eating, while walking, once while canoeing, and which she defended so fiercely that the other girls had begun to impugn her whole personality, saying she cared more about pages than people. Kaitlyn didn't think that was fair. Mira noticed things. It was Mira who had said the lake looked like two lakes, and she had said it not to be cruel but the way a person reports the weather.

From where Mira sat, the painting's problem was obvious, though she didn't yet have a word for it. She set down her brush, wiped her hands on her shorts, and pulled the top book off her stack, a fat one with a cracked spine called The Chemistry of Color. She liked this book because it treated paint as a substance with a history, and because it never once told her what to feel. She turned pages with her thumb, past chapters on pigments and dyes, until she reached a portrait of a man with side-whiskers and a severe collar. She read a while, then carried the book over.

"Look at this," Mira said. "A chemist. Michel Eugène Chevreul. He ran the dye works at a tapestry factory, and the weavers kept blaming the dyers for colors that came out wrong, and he figured out it was neither of them. He published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839. It says a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. So your gray next to the orange tents shifts toward blue, and the same gray next to the green pines shifts toward red. Orange and blue are complements. Green and red are complements. That's your two lakes."

Kaitlyn looked from the book to the canvas and back. It was like someone handing her glasses she hadn't known she needed. The lake wasn't broken and she wasn't careless; the gray was doing what any color did, whether or not the painter understood why. She thought of asking Mira why it worked that way, what happened in the eye, but the book was already sliding shut and Mira was already saying she had a dragonfly to finish.

"Can I borrow it tonight?" Kaitlyn asked.

"It's due at the Halloway library the day I get home, so it's basically in my fiduciary care," Mira said. "But yes. Just don't get paint on page ninety."

Kaitlyn spent the rest of the afternoon deciding what to do with what she now knew. One path was to fight the effect, to repaint the tents gray-blue and the pines gray-red until the lake read as one lake no matter what sat beside it. Another path was to keep it, even to use it, letting the water warm where the tents were and cool where the trees were, the way the actual lake held two skies at once on windy days. She tried the second way first, adding a thin wash of green over the right half, and then she sat on the floor with her back against the easel leg and considered whether she was solving the problem or decorating it. The truth was she couldn't tell yet. The fact that Chevreul had a law didn't tell her what her painting wanted. Laws described; they didn't decide.

By dinner she had repainted the tents a paler, quieter orange and let the water alone. Ruby walked the rows of easels with a clipboard, saying "dry, dry, still tacky" like a person taking attendance. When she reached Kaitlyn's canvas she stopped, tilted her head, and looked a long time at the lake.

"Some kind of metamorphic thing?" Ruby asked. "Water changing into rock?"

"Something like that," Kaitlyn said.

That night in the cabin, after lights out, Mira passed the book across the gap between the bunks. Kaitlyn read by the green glow of the clock, turning pages carefully, stopping at the portrait with the side-whiskers. She read the same paragraph three times. Then she set the book on the floor between the bunks where neither of them owned it, and lay listening to the actual lake below the hill, which held whatever colors it held regardless of anyone's law, and in the morning she would look at the canvas and decide.

Mira, from the top bunk, said into the dark, "Page ninety is still clean."

"I know," Kaitlyn said. "I checked."

Megan had chosen the bowling alley because it was impossible to sit across from someone there in silence for two hours. You had to get up, pick a ball, walk back, let the machine do its loud arithmetic. The structure did half the work for you, and she suspected she would need that, because the boy, Dmitri, had seemed nervous at the coffee shop earlier, stirring his cappuccino long after the foam had dissolved.

The trouble was that the structure was not enough. By the third frame they had covered siblings, intended majors, the weather in a way that felt like a hostage negotiation. Dmitri bowled a strike and then a gutter ball and apologized to the gutter ball. Megan laughed, genuinely, and then the air went flat again, and she understood that if she did not do something, the whole evening would become a polite countdown.

"There's this thing," she said, sitting down beside him in the plastic seats. "This study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and afterward they felt closer than pairs who just made small talk." She spun her water bottle on the floor with one finger. "We could try it. Half of it, anyway. We're strangers, technically."

"We met at a pre-orientation thing," Dmitri said.

"Technically."

He looked at her for a moment, and she had the feeling of being weighed by someone who was not used to doing the weighing. "Okay," he said. "But if it works, I get to say I knew you before you were famous."

"Question one," she said, and then had to admit she didn't remember the actual list, which was either a flaw in her plan or the thing that made it hers. "We'll make up our own. What's something you wanted to be when you were a kid that you'd never tell anyone now?"

They went slowly at first, trading questions between turns, and Megan found something she had not expected: the questions worked better when they were bad ones. Dmitri asked her what she was afraid of and she gave the prepared answer, spiders, and then he asked what she was afraid of in a way she couldn't pretend about, and she said failing publicly at something she'd told people she was good at, and he nodded like a person recognizing a house on a street he lived on. His father had been a musician in Bulgaria, he told her at the seventh frame, before they emigrated, and there was a consonance between that fact and the way he held the ball, some attention in the wrists, and she almost said so but decided the observation could stay hers.

By the ninth frame she had learned that he wanted to study architecture but was signed up for economics, and that he had not told his parents this, and that he was more frightened of their sadness than their anger. She told him about her sister, the one she'd mentioned at the coffee shop, that they hadn't spoken since March, and that Megan had written eleven drafts of a text and sent none of them, and that she kept thinking she could resuscitate the relationship with some perfect message when the truth was she didn't know if her sister wanted to be brought back. Dmitri listened without performing listening, nonodding theatrics, which she noted and filed away. He was, she decided, the kind of perspicacious person who didn't advertise it, and that was rarer than she'd expected to find at eighteen.

"So do you feel closer?" she asked, when they'd run through maybe twenty of their thirty-six and her questions had stopped being strategic and started being things she actually wanted answered. "Like the study said. Closer than small talk."

Dmitri rolled his ball, watched it curve toward the pocket, and missed everything by a margin so complete it was almost skillful. "I think the study's real," he said. "I also think you already knew it would be, or you wouldn't have suggested it. Which was pretty perspicacious of you, actually."

"You don't get to use my word."

"Your word?"

She stood, picked up her ball, and walked to the line, and behind her she heard him say her name once, experimentally, like testing the weight of a borrowed instrument. She swung her arm back, let it go, and the ball rolled straight down the middle of the lane and knocked down exactly one pin, the far corner one, left side, and they both watched it fall.

The biology test was on Friday, and Sadie had promised Mr. Okafor she would run the review session for the students who'd failed the first one. She'd volunteered in a moment of confidence she no longer possessed, standing in his classroom after the bell, and now it was Wednesday and she had to actually do it.

"They don't want another lecture," Mr. Okafor had said, handing her a shoebox of index cards. "Do something where they move around. The community garden's free fourth period."

So at fourth period Sadie stood in the garden between the rain barrel and the rows of turgid lettuce, the leaves still stiff and glistening from the morning watering, and laid her cards out on the bench. Six students showed up, which was five more than she expected, including Deni, who had failed spectacularly and did not care who knew it.

"Okay," she said. "Translation. We're going to be it."

Deni folded his arms. "Be it how?"

She gave one student a long strip of paper with three letters on it, CGA, and had her stand by the tomato stakes. "You're the messenger RNA. You're the message that got copied from the DNA, and you're just going to stand there and be read." Then she dealt out the other cards, each one folded in half: three big letters on top, a single amino acid name written inside. "Everyone else is a transfer RNA."

"Who named these things," Deni muttered, looking at his card.

"Nobody important. Look, open it." His card read UCA on the outside, and inside, in her own handwriting, serine. She took his wrist and walked him to the messenger. "Your letters are the anticodon. Read hers and find the match."

He stood in front of the strip, scowling, moving his lips. Then he turned his card sideways, then right side up, until the letters lined up opposite the three on the messenger's paper. He handed over the amino acid name and looked at her, waiting.

"That's it," Sadie said. "You matched your anticodon to her codon, and the amino acid you were carrying gets handed over. That's a transfer RNA doing its whole job. You carry one amino acid, you match three bases, you add your piece." She pointed at the next student. "Go."

It worked, in a stumbling way. One girl held her card upside down until Deni snapped at her about the direction. A boy tried to hand over two amino acid cards at once because he wanted to finish faster, and Sadie took the second one back. "One each," she said. "You carry one. That's the whole deal." He shrugged and matched his three letters, and the chain of paper strips along the bench grew: methionine, serine, leucine, a small dumb word being spelled out by people shuffling around a garden.

She was pleased, briefly, until Deni said, "So who decided the message?"

"Nobody decided it. It got copied from the DNA."

"No, but who decided the DNA?" He tapped the messenger's strip. "Somebody wanted it to say that."

"It's not about wanting. It's chemistry." Sadie heard how turgid her own voice sounded, teacherly and stiff, and she heard too that she was starting to equivocate, saying maybe and sort of, backing away from a question she'd asked herself at two in the morning. In the textbook there was no wanting. In the textbook, things copied themselves and got read and built things, and the chain got longer, and somewhere a cell did what a cell does. But standing here watching Deni's card pass from his hand to the bench, she could see why he thought there had to be a purpose underneath it, some intention steering the whole business toward its result. She'd caught herself thinking the same thing, folding the cards at her desk, imagining the message wanted to become a protein.

"That's called teleology," said Priya, from the end of the bench, matching her last anticodon. "When you explain things by their purpose instead of their causes. My sister's doing it in philosophy."

"I wasn't explaining anything," Deni said.

"You were asking."

He had no answer for that, and neither did Sadie, exactly. The chain was complete now, all the amino acids laid in order, and the six of them stood around it in the wet grass. It was a real thing they had made, a word spelled by hands, and it had happened without anyone wanting it to, and also she had planned every step. Both of those were true and she could not make them be the same truth.

"Friday," she said, gathering the cards. "Same questions. You'll know the answers."

"Will you?" Deni asked.

She squared the cards against the bench and put them back in the shoebox. "Ask me after the test."

Olivier had promised himself he would start the essay on Sunday, and it was now Tuesday, and the draft folder on his laptop held one sentence: "Historians have disagreed about the French Revolution." He sat at the kitchen table with the window open to a crepuscular evening, the sort of light that made everything in the room look provisional, as if the furniture were only trying out its positions. The essay was due Thursday. He had four historians' articles printed and highlighted, and he had read them the way you read a train timetable, hunting for what he needed and skipping the rest.

His grandfather, who had come to stay for the week while the radiators were being replaced in his own flat, shuffled in and set down two mugs of tea. He had a way of moving through a room as though narrating it to himself. On the table he also placed a parcel wrapped in a plastic bag from a bookshop that had closed years ago.

"You left this behind last summer," he said. "My shelf. I found it when I was looking for my tax receipts, which I still have not found, so this is my only achievement of the week."

Inside the bag was a fat, foxed volume with the spine held on by tape. The French Revolution: A History, by Thomas Carlyle, published in 1837, the title page said, in that self-important Victorian type. Olivier had seen the name in one of his articles, cited in a footnote like a relative nobody invited but who shows up anyway.

"Is this the Carlyle?" he asked. "The one my essay's supposed to mention?"

"Published in 1837," his grandfather said, tapping the page. "He wrote it after the thing itself, mind, so he was doing what you're doing. Looking back."

Olivier opened it at random and found a chapter in which a member of the National Assembly trembled at a doorway, and the doorway was described for a full paragraph, and somewhere a bell tolled. He tried to take notes. His pen hovered. "He's not arguing anything," he complained. "He's doing weather."

"He cared about people's souls," his grandfather said, settling into the chair opposite. "What they chose, what they refused to choose."

Olivier wrote that down, then crossed it out, then wrote it again smaller. The four printed historians, by contrast, talked about structures, about fiscal crises and bread prices and the logic of institutions, as though the Revolution were a machine that had behaved exactly as its design required. One of them used the word "utilitarianism" as an accusation, claiming that a certain school of historians judged the Terror by arithmetic alone, bodies counted against outcomes, and that this told you more about the historians than about the Terror. Olivier underlined it twice and then felt embarrassed about underlining twice, as though the page could see him.

He worked past nine. His grandfather went to bed and could be heard negotiating with the spare room's radiator, which gurgled like a creature with opinions. Olivier kept reading Carlyle, one chapter, then another, waiting for the drama to resolve into an argument, and it never did, and slowly he understood that the drama was the argument. Carlyle, in 1837, stressed the moral choices of individuals rather than impersonal historical forces: Mirabeau deciding, Danton deciding, a seamstress deciding whether to shout. Where the modern historians saw a system producing consequences, Carlyle saw people who could have done otherwise. That, Olivier realized, was the hinge the whole question turned on, and it underwrote two centuries of disagreement more quietly than any of the articles had admitted. It was not that one side had better evidence. It was that they disagreed about what counted as an explanation at all.

He typed a new first sentence, deleted it, typed another. At half past eleven his phone buzzed: his classmate Iris, who had claimed since year ten that she worked best under panic. "Have you started," she wrote, without a question mark. "Carlyle's style is insane," he sent back. "It's all bells and doorways." "Bells and doorways," she replied. "Put that in the essay. Markers love a vendetta." He laughed, alone, quietly, so as not to wake anyone, and it was the first time all evening the work had felt like something other than duty.

By one in the morning he had a page and a half. It argued that historians after Carlyle had reacted against him, that they had built their impersonal forces precisely to escape his drama, and that maybe both were partly right, though he could not yet say how a person could be partly a force. That part he left as a question in the text, flagged with a bracket he suspected he would not remove. The conclusion was unwritten. He wrote at the bottom of the page, "Some of this stays open," and looked at it for a while.

In the morning his grandfather found him asleep on the printed articles, the Carlyle open on the floor beside him, one taped corner of the spine having finally given up. He bent, with some ceremony, and picked it up. "I'll get the tape," he said. Olivier, not quite awake, answered from inside his folded arms, "Keep it for me. I might need the doorways again."

The kitchen table had become Chase's desk by seven o'clock, his chemistry textbook propped against the salt shaker, a worksheet facedown beside his elbow like something he was pretending not to have finished. His mother had left a mug of tea at the far end, still too hot, the steam drifting toward him in a way that felt like an offered truce. He had gotten the first two problems right, or mostly right, and the third had gone wrong in a manner he couldn't locate, which was worse than being lost entirely. He pulled the worksheet toward him and read it again.

The problem gave him forty-eight grams of magnesium reacting with oxygen, and asked for the mass of magnesium oxide produced. The balanced equation sat in his notes, copied from the board in Ms. Ferreira's looping hand: two Mg plus O two, arrow, two MgO. He had set up his proportion the way that seemed obvious, forty-eight grams over two, equals x grams over two, and arrived at forty-eight grams of product, which the answer line in the back of the book did not agree with. The back of the book wanted eighty grams. He checked his arithmetic twice, then a third time, and the arithmetic was blameless, which meant the fault lay somewhere upstream of the arithmetic, in the setup itself, and he had no idea where.

His younger sister, Dahlia, padded in from the living room in her socks and stood at the counter eating cereal from a box, which she did when she was stalling on her own homework. She watched him scratch out a line. "You look like Dad when the printer breaks," she said. She was eleven and had recently discovered that observation was a form of power.

"Big words from someone eating dry cereal out of the box." He said it without heat, because she had, without being asked, slid the box down the counter toward him, and he took a handful, and the small exchange felt like a rope thrown across a gap. He chewed and stared at the equation. Two over two equaled one over one, so the ratio changed nothing, which meant that if the masses were supposed to be equal they would be equal, and they weren't, and so the ratio of the equation must not be a ratio of masses at all.

He turned back to the textbook, past the worked example he'd skipped in his hurry, to a paragraph about molar mass. Magnesium, twenty-four grams per mole. Oxygen, sixteen. Magnesium oxide, forty. He sat with those numbers the way you sit with a person you've misjudged. Forty-eight grams of magnesium was two moles of magnesium. Two moles. The equation's coefficients, the big twos in front of Mg and MgO, were twos of something, and he had used them as twos of grams, and those were not the same thing at all.

"So the twos in the equation," he said aloud, half to Dahlia, half to the tea, "are moles, not grams." She looked at him over the cereal box. "The coefficients in a balanced equation give you the ratio of moles that react," he said, slowly, testing each word as he set it down, "not the ratio of masses." Nobody had told him that today, exactly; Ms. Ferreira had said it on Tuesday while he was copying the equation and not listening to the sentence around it, and he recognized it now the way you recognize a face in a crowd an hour too late.

He redid the problem on a fresh sheet. Two moles of magnesium would produce two moles of magnesium oxide, because the ratio was two to two, mole to mole. Two moles of magnesium oxide at forty grams per mole was eighty grams. The back of the book agreed with him for the first time all evening, and he sat back and let the agreement settle, wanting to preempt his own relief, because he knew that a right answer gotten once was not a right answer gotten always. He had made an assumption that felt natural and it had been wrong in a way that was almost elegant, a ratio that looked like a ratio and measured something else entirely.

His father came in from the garage with his jacket half off and looked at the papers spread across the table, and Chase preempted the question by turning the sheet around. "I was using grams where I needed moles," he said. "Masses don't travel through the equation. Moles do." His father picked up the paper, read it, and set it down with the judicious slowness of a man who had taken exactly one semester of chemistry in 1989 and knew the limits of his authority. "That's more than I could tell you," he said. "But you look like you mean it."

"I mean it and I'm maybe sixty percent sure I could do it again cold," Chase said, and his father nodded as though sixty percent were an honest number, which it was, and honesty about uncertainty was, in their house, a currency that held its value better than bluffing. Dahlia had drifted back to the doorway with the cereal box under her arm. "You're talking to yourself now," she said. "Only a little," he said, and reached for the next problem on the sheet.

The laminated menu at Il Forno had a crease down the middle, and Dylan kept folding it back along that line while Mr. Petrossian read his one-page application. "You wrote your availability as, quote, whenever." Mr. Petrossian looked up. "That is not a schedule. That is a cry for help."

"It's enthusiasm," Dylan said. "It's exuding from me."

"It's exuding all over my floor, is what it is. Can you carry four plates?" Dylan said probably, and was immediately handed four plates, warm from the pass, and told to walk them to table nine and back. He walked them. He did not drop them, though the bread plate made a slow rotation the whole way, like a planet with doubts. Mr. Petrossian watched, chewed the inside of his cheek, and said he could start Friday, four to close, and to buy non-slip shoes before he killed somebody, probably himself.

That night Dylan did the arithmetic on a napkin, because his mother had told him that if he was going to work, he should know what he was being paid, and arithmetic was the only part of that he could do alone. Six hours Friday, six Saturday, at eleven an hour. He wrote 132 and drew a box around it, then a second box, celebratory. But Rosa, who had bussed tables at Il Forno for two years and sat behind him in study hall, leaned across the aisle and squinted at his napkin. "That's not your check," she said. "Watch."

She texted him a photo of her own pay stub, small gray numbers she'd had to zoom in on, with a row that said SOC SEC and a row that said MED, and next to SOC SEC a percentage. "What's that?" he typed back. "Social Security," she answered. "Employers withhold 6.2 percent of your wages for it, up to a yearly wage limit. After the limit they stop for the year." He read it twice, then did the subtraction on the napkin, then looked at the number, which was his 132 minus six point two percent of 132, minus some other things Rosa called "the government's appetizer," and which no longer felt like 132 at all.

"But wait," he said Monday, catching her at her locker, "so it comes back to me someday?" Rosa shrugged in the specific way of someone who had asked her father the same question at fifteen and gotten a lecture. "Someday it's like an annuity, a stream of payments when you're old. That's the idea, anyway. Whether the idea holds up by the time we're old," and here she made a noise like a deflating tire, "is above my pay grade. Which, as you now know, is smaller than my pay grade."

Dylan carried this around for a few days the way he carried the plates, aware of its weight without fully knowing where to set it down. On one hand, six point two percent was his, earned, gone before it touched his pocket, and that struck him as a kind of theft with paperwork. On the other hand, his grandmother collected a check every month, had for years, and paid for her prescriptions with it, and that was not theoretical, that was a Tuesday. Both things were true at once, which was annoying. He could hold both, he decided, the way he'd held the four plates: carefully, with a certain rotation, and without pretending any of them wasn't there.

His first Friday, the kitchen extruded a perfect ribbon of pappardelle through the pasta machine, and Chef held it up to the light and said, "Beautiful, no? You see this, new boy, this is craft. You will never learn it. You will carry plates." At the register, the ancient credit card machine wheezed through each transaction, and Rosa patted it and called it obsolescent, "but it's mine, and it's never once dropped a card, unlike some people and their bread plates." Dylan said the bread plate rotation had been intentional, a flourish. Rosa said, "Do the flourish toward table two, they're waving, and congratulations, you now know exactly how much this flourish is costing you."

He picked up the pad, wrote table two at the top, and walked over with his pen already clicking. "Good evening," he said. "Can I start you off with something to drink?"

Sadie spread the battered paperback open on the kitchen table and set a pad of paper beside it, square and blank as a dare. Her summer assignment was due in eleven days: apply a critical lens to three chapters of a classic novel. She had chosen the lens off a list in the course packet, half because the word "Marxist" looked serious, half because her older cousin Priya, who had taken the same class two years ago, had leaned across the graduation party and said, "Pick that one. It will wreck how you read everything." That sounded like a promise and a warning at once, and Sadie had signed up for both.

The novel she had chosen was Austen, the one everyone claimed to love. On a first pass she had read it the way she read everything, at speed, skating across the surfaces of drawing rooms and errands and proposals. Now the packet told her to slow down and read with a question in her mouth. She found the question in the second page of notes: a Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible. It told her to notice the servants the novel mentions only in passing. Sadie sat back. She tried to remember a single servant from the whole book and could not.

So she tried something clumsy and literal. She went back to the first chapter she'd flagged and began counting on her fingers, then on paper, making a tally in the margin every time a servant was named. The housekeeper, the cook, a maid dispatched with a note: four times in one chapter, named, useful, folded into the machinery of the day. Then a second tally, for speech. She drew the column and waited for a mark to put in it. She reached the end of the chapter with the column still empty. In an entire chapter of talk, of people explaining themselves at length, no one who worked in that house said a single word on the page.
