Historians argue about Vindolanda all the time. They disagree about what the tablets even mean, because the sources are partial and because we keep asking new questions of them. My textbook from two years ago called the frontier soldiers bored and bureaucratic. A paper I read last week called them a community. Same tablets."

"So which is it?" Devon asked.

"Both, probably. Or it depends on what you're asking." She looked down at Claudia Severa's handwriting, the part that was hers. "Nobody gets to be absolved from judging, that's all. You look at what survived, you admit what didn't, and you say something careful."

The bell was five minutes off. Mr. Rowley asked, mildly, whether Faith would hand in her essay on supply records as planned, since the invitation was rather off topic. Faith looked at the photocopied tablet one more time, at the slant of the closing lines where a woman had picked up the pen herself to add something warm and personal after the scribe's formal part was done.

"Can I write about this instead?" she said.

Rowley's mouth twitched. "Two thousand words. And cite the disagreement, not just the tablet."

Faith folded the page again, along its old creases, and Priya leaned over and asked if she could copy it. Outside, the wind bent the last maple branch flat against the glass.

"Take a picture," Faith said, and held it up to the light.

The kitchen table still smelled of the onions her father had chopped at noon, and Sophia had pushed the cutting board to one end to make room for the score, her headphones, and a legal pad with three columns ruled in blue ink: exposition, development, recapitulation. On Monday she would stand at a piano in a room with two examiners and mark the form of the Mozart movement out loud, bar by bar, and if she hesitated for more than a few seconds they would move on without her. She had until Sunday night.

She played the opening thirty seconds four times. The first theme arrived like someone stepping into a room already mid-sentence, and she wrote its bars in the first column, then the second theme, lyrical, in a different key, the way her textbook said it must be. That was the exposition. She underlined it twice, judicious about the ink, and moved on.

The middle section defeated her. She had listened to it six times that week, and each time it slid past her pencil. It was stormy, constantly changing, and she could not find where one theme ended and another began. Her notes from Tuesday read, in increasingly cramped handwriting, "everything moves," then "can't tell what's happening," then nothing. By Thursday a flat ennui had settled over the project, the specific tiredness of a task that refuses to open itself, and she had left the score on the table and gone to bed early, which she never did.

On Friday afternoon a letter came. Not email, an actual envelope, forwarded from the music school, from a girl named Priya Raghavan who had taken the same entrance analysis two years ago and now sat on the student panel that reviewed applications. "I heard you're doing the Mozart," she wrote, in slanted ballpoint. "Everyone panics at the middle. I did too. The examiners aren't testing whether you can name every bar. They're testing whether you can hear when the music stops being sure of itself. When it stops being sure, that's where you look." At the bottom, after her signature, she had added: "It's more honest than you think. Trust your ears over your notes."

Sophia read the letter twice at the mailbox, in the cold, and then carried it inside and propped it against the pepper grinder where she could see it.

That evening her grandmother called from the nursing home, as she did every Friday, and Sophia, instead of the usual five minutes, carried the phone to the table and told her about the middle section. "It sounds like the first theme got caught in a wind," she said. "Pieces of it flying around, landing somewhere new every second."

Her grandmother was quiet a moment, and then, because she had played until arthritis ended it, she said only, "Restless. That's the sound they want you to name." She asked about the weather in Ohio and hung up without ceremony, the way she did everything.

Sophia put the headphones back on. Seventh listen, eighth. She stopped trying to write anything and closed her eyes, and near the start of the stormy section she heard it: four notes she recognized, a fragment of the opening tune, the exact shape of it, but brief, snatched away almost before she could point at it, and then it turned up again in a different key, then lower, then somewhere she couldn't have named, each appearance shorter than the last. The movement wasn't lost at all. It was taking its own themes apart and carrying the pieces quickly through key after key, and the restlessness she'd been fighting was the method itself. She opened her eyes and wrote, in the second column, "fragments of theme 1, several keys, fast." Then she listened once more and caught the lyrical second theme in there too, broken and sped up and made strange, transmuted from something singing into something searching.

She worked until ten, marking where the fragments gave way to the return, the opening theme arriving whole again in the home key, and she wrote recapitulation and underlined it once. At the piano in her living room, which nobody had tuned since spring, she played the four notes of the fragment, then the full theme, hearing how the one had been hiding inside the other all week.

The last thing she did before bed was take Priya's letter to her room. On Sunday she would speak the whole analysis aloud to the examiners, and she did not know yet whether her marking was right, whether the second theme's return came where she'd placed it or four bars later, whether she would keep her voice steady. The uncertain bars she had flagged with small question marks, and she decided she would leave them there, and say so if asked. She turned off the lamp, and on the dark ceiling the three columns floated behind her eyes, the middle one full.

Gabrielle had counted the money twice on the bus: forty-two dollars, the exact price of the ticket printed on the flyer, tucked into the pocket of her work apron before her shift. She had her first paycheque folded in the same pocket, and on the break-room table she smoothed it flat and read it like a message in a language she almost knew. Gross pay: 512 dollars. She had worked the hours herself, sixty-four of them over three weeks at eight dollars an hour, and the arithmetic was clean. Net pay: 413.77. Somewhere between the two numbers, nearly a hundred dollars had gone, itemized in small print: federal income tax, state income tax, something called FICA. She understood, in a general way, that this was how the government funded itself, but seeing it subtracted line by line from her own money felt different from knowing it in the abstract. It was like the difference between knowing rain existed and standing in it.

"First one?" Danielle asked, sliding into the seat across from her with a container of noodles. Danielle was twenty-two and had worked at Harmon's Market for five years, long enough to have opinions about everything and to deliver them while eating.

"They took out income tax," Gabrielle said. "I thought my parents just did that in April."

"You file in April to settle up. The paycheque is where they take it." Danielle tapped the deductions column with her chopstick. "Sometimes you get some back. That's the refund."

"Wait. They take it, and then they give it back?"

"If they took too much. It depends on what you made all year." Danielle shrugged, as if this were a system designed by weather rather than by people.

The break room had one window, and through it Gabrielle could see the parking lot going gold with late afternoon. She turned the paycheque over, as though the reverse might explain the front. It didn't, but she noticed something else on the stub: a smaller line for the employee contribution to dental, twelve dollars she had apparently agreed to and didn't remember agreeing to. She would ask about that later. For now, the ticket money was the urgent thing, and after her shift she planned to walk straight to the record store two blocks over, where the flyer in the window said forty-two dollars, Saturday show, all ages.

The problem arrived at register four at 6:40, ten minutes before she could clock out, when she was covering for Marcus's break. A boy about her age, maybe a year younger, came through her lane with a box of granola bars and a comic book and laid his money on the counter: exact change, which he had clearly counted with great care, because it was arranged in stacks, quarters on quarters, like a small igneous formation layered under pressure over time. She rang the items and the screen showed the total. It was higher than the sticker prices added together. She looked at the difference, then at his stacks, then at the screen again.

"Sales tax," she said slowly, mostly to herself, watching the register add it on top of the posted prices rather than include it in them.

"I don't have more," the boy said. His voice was flat, not angry, the voice of someone who had already done all the math he could do. "The bars are four dollars and the comic is six. That's ten. I have ten."

"I know. The prices on the shelf, they're before tax. It gets added here." She pointed at the screen. "So the total comes out higher than what's posted." She heard the sentence leave her mouth and understood it fully for the first time as she said it, the way you sometimes understand a word only when you have to define it to someone else.

He looked at the granola bars for a long moment and then slid the comic back toward her. "Just the bars, then." She voided the comic, took four dollars plus the thirty-some cents of tax, and watched him pocket his remaining quarters. He said thanks. She watched him walk out past the flyers in the front window, hands in his jacket, and she thought about her own forty-two dollars sitting in her apron, and about what the record store's register would do to it.

When Danielle passed on her way to stock dairy, Gabrielle called her over. "If the ticket is forty-two, how much do I actually need?"

Danielle did it in her head, round numbers. "Call it forty-five to be safe. Why, do you have exactly forty-two?"

"I have exactly forty-two."

"Then you, my friend, are one sales tax short of a Saturday night." Danielle laughed, but not unkindly, and kept walking.

Gabrielle finished the register close-out, and while she counted the drawer she kept circling the same thought from different directions. Her paycheque had been reduced by taxes she hadn't felt herself paying; the boy's money had been reduced by a tax he hadn't known was coming; both of them had walked in believing a posted number that turned out to be only part of the truth. She had spent her whole life being told prices, and only now did it occur to her to wonder how many other systems worked this way, the visible number and the real number, with the difference surfacing only at the moment of payment. Maybe the deductions were the same thing at a slower speed. Maybe they weren't. She hadn't decided yet whether the whole arrangement was reasonable, or whether a hidden cost was a kind of disincentive to ever trusting a shelf price again, and she suspected the honest answer was that she didn't have enough information to judge, only enough to notice.

She clocked out and walked to the record store with the streetlights coming on. At the counter she laid out her forty-two dollars, then dug deeper into her backpack, found a five folded into a pocket she'd forgotten, and put that down too. The clerk rang it up and slid the ticket and the receipt across the counter, the receipt showing the ticket price and then, beneath it, the tax, and then the total, and she read all three lines before folding it into her pocket next to the paycheque stub.

"You're the first person all day to actually look at the receipt," the clerk said.

"I'm learning how the numbers work," Gabrielle said, and picked up her ticket.

The retake was on Tuesday, and Eva had until then to understand something she had memorized but never actually grasped. Her quiz came back with a red circle around question four: why does the cell not send DNA itself out to make protein? She had written, in a moment of panic, because DNA is too important, which turned out to be true and useless at the same time, the way a lot of true things were. Mrs. Okafor had written see me in the margin, and Eva had not gone, because going would mean admitting she could recite the steps in order and still not know what any of them were for.

On Saturday her mother drove her out to Uncle Ravi's farm to help with the new lambs, which was supposed to be a break from school and instead became the place where school finally happened. Her cousin Dean was ten, tall for his age, and in the middle of a campaign to be told everything about everything. When Eva sat down on an overturned bucket in the barn, he asked her what the folder in her jacket was.

"Biology," she said. "I'm failing it."

"You're eighteen," Dean said, as if that settled the matter of what a person should be able to do.

One of the lambs had gotten separated from its mother and was being bottle-fed by Uncle Ravi, who held the bottle at an angle and let the animal pull rather than pushing milk into its mouth. Dean watched this for a while and then said, apropos of nothing Eva could detect, "How does a lamb know how to be a lamb?"

"It's in the instructions," Eva said. "In the cells."

"Then where are the instructions? Show me one."

She looked at the lamb, at its wet nose pushing against the rubber nipple, and found that she could not answer him without answering herself. "They're in the middle of the cell," she said slowly. "In the DNA. And the DNA stays there. It doesn't go out."

"Why not? If it's got the instructions."

Eva opened her folder. Her quiz was still in it, question four circled in red, and she sat with it on her knee while the barn smelled of straw and iodine dip and the heater rattled in the corner. She thought about the library, which was how she had been taught to think about DNA, a room full of original books that no one was allowed to remove. Then she thought: you don't rip a page out of the library. You make a copy and carry the copy.

"Because it makes a copy," she said. "Like if you had a recipe in a book and you didn't want to get the book dirty in the kitchen. You'd write the recipe on a slip of paper and take that instead."

Dean considered this. "That's a photocopy."

"Sort of. There's an enzyme, RNA polymerase, that does the copying. It reads one strand of the DNA and builds a matching strand of messenger RNA."

"Messenger," Dean repeated, with the satisfaction of a word that explained itself. "It carries the message out."

"Right. It carries the gene's instructions out to where the protein gets made." Even as she said it, she could feel the whole unit reassembling itself in her head, transcription and translation snapping into position like the panels of a gate she had been trying to force shut the wrong way. The copy went out, was read, was used, and was thrown away, and the original never left the barn. The library stayed intact. The recipe stayed clean.

Monday night she sat at the kitchen table drawing it out, arrow by arrow, refusing to look at the textbook until she had finished, and then comparing. She had the direction right. What she could not decide, even after twenty minutes, was whether to tell Mrs. Okafor that she had learned it from a ten-year-old and a lamb, or whether that admission would augur badly for her credibility. Probably, she decided, it was fine to leave the lamb out.

Tuesday's retake had the same question four, reworded but not disguised. Eva wrote that the cell keeps the DNA in the nucleus and sends out a working copy, a strand of messenger RNA built by RNA polymerase reading one strand of the DNA, because the instructions need to travel without the original leaving. She read it over twice. It was strange, she thought, that her first attempt had not been wrong so much as a travesty of an answer, a shape with none of the machinery inside it, and that the machinery had only shown up once someone had demanded it of her in a barn. Her nascent understanding, she had to admit, was still understanding of a particular kind: she could explain it to a ten-year-old, and she was no longer sure that was a limitation.

She handed the paper in, and on her way out passed the terrarium by the door where the biology classes kept the crickets, one of which was, at that moment, singing against the glass.

The waiting room of Adeyemi & Associates smelled of toner and the burnt edge of someone's microwaved lunch. Riley sat across from a woman flipping through a shoebox of receipts, and next to a fish tank whose single occupant had the truculent look of someone who had also been asked to wait. He had his own folder on his knees: his first paycheques from the hardware store, his T4 slip, and a coffee-stained receipt from the art supply shop where he'd bought canvas board for a mural job he'd done for the camera shop downtown.

His mother had made the appointment. "You earned real money this year," she'd said, in the voice she used for vaccinations, "so you get to do real paperwork." His summer and Saturdays at the hardware store had paid him just over nine thousand dollars, and every two weeks his paycheque had arrived with a smaller number than the one he'd arithmetic'd in his head on the walk home. The missing chunk was itemized on the stub in a column labelled income tax, deducted at source, which he'd assumed for the first month was some kind of clerical insult before his coworker Denny explained that everybody's cheque arrived already nibbled.

"Adeyemi will see you now," said the receptionist, who was also his mother's friend Pauline, which was how the appointment had cost nothing.

Mr. Adeyemi's office had two chairs, a monitor, and a framed print of a sailing ship that had clearly never been questioned. He waved Riley toward the second chair and rotated the screen toward him. "You've done most of it already, I see. You entered your wages. Good. Now, this box here, and this one here." He tapped the screen twice. "You can only use one of these this year. Take your time."

Riley leaned in. The software showed his mural income, four hundred dollars, and then two boxes. One said deduction, eligible expenses, and the number in it was larger. The other said credit, and the number was smaller. He'd already internalized the general principle that in life you took the larger number: the bigger slice, the longer lie-in, the extra fries. He checked the deduction box.

The tax owing at the bottom of the screen went down a little. He frowned, unchecked it, and tried the credit instead.

The tax owing went down a lot. By more. Even though the number attached to it was smaller. He sat back, checked the deduction again, watched the smaller drop, then flipped back to the credit and watched the bigger one, like a man comparing two photographs of the same suspect.

"Huh," he said.

"Something?" Mr. Adeyemi was signing something else, a stack of envelopes, and did not look up.

"The little number does more than the big number."

"Mm," said Mr. Adeyemi, in the tone of a man who had heard this sentence several thousand times and never tired of hearing it again, the way an epicure never tires of bread.

Riley looked at the screen for a while longer. So the deduction lowered the income that the tax was calculated on, and the credit subtracted straight from the tax itself, and that was why the credit was worth more than a deduction of the same size. He said this last part out loud, slowly, testing it, the way you'd test ice. "So a credit's usually worth more than an equal deduction."

"Usually," said Mr. Adeyemi, and stampeded no further into explanation, which Riley found he appreciated. It was like Denny that time with the paycheque stub: one sentence, then let the kid do his own staring.

The receipt question came next, and this one Riley had partly worked out at home. He spread his art supply receipt on the desk. The canvas board had cost $18.50 at the till, and below that a line read HST, and then a total of $20.96. He'd known about sales tax since he was seven and had brought a loonie to the dollar store and been humiliated at the register, but he'd never connected it to anything until he needed it on paper. "This is sales tax," he said. "It's on the receipt. It's on basically everything I buy."

"It is," said Mr. Adeyemi. "And unlike your income tax, it doesn't come back to you in April. It's just gone. Consider it rent on being a person who buys things." He said it drily, without looking up from his envelopes.

Riley filed the receipt in the right place, typed his municipal tax account number with one finger, and then sat with his hands still on the keyboard. He'd come in assuming taxes were a single thing, one big bite, and he was leaving with at least three: the income tax that had been coming off his cheques all year, the sales tax that came off at the till where nobody wrote him a receipt for it, and this difference between deductions and credits that had made him choose wrong on the first try and would have made him choose wrong forever, cheerfully, taking the bigger number every time. He still wasn't sure what he thought about any of it, except that the paycheque stubs in his folder looked different now, less like insults and more like instalments on a bill he hadn't yet been shown.

"Am I done?" he asked.

"You're done. You'll get some of it back, they took a bit more than they needed to." Mr. Adeyemi slid the envelopes aside and finally looked at him. "First refund is a rite of passage. Try not to spend it all at once."

"Can't," Riley said, zipping his folder. "There's tax on spending."

Pauline laughed from the front desk, one syllable, not unkind. Riley put his hand on the door handle, and behind him Mr. Adeyemi said, quietly, to the envelopes or to the room, "He'll do fine."

Ava spread the two pay stubs side by side on the kitchen table, hers first, then Priya's, which had arrived as a photo on her phone and was now printed, slightly blurry, on the family's ancient printer. Both of them had started jobs in July, Ava at the grocery store in Ottawa and Priya at a bakery in Montreal, and both had been shocked by their first paycheques. Ava had counted on four hundred dollars and received three hundred and forty-one. She was saving for a laptop before college started, and she needed to know exactly where the fifty-nine dollars had gone, because if it kept disappearing, the laptop would slip from August into October.

"You too?" Priya had said on the phone that morning, sounding morose in the way she got when numbers disappointed her. "Mine's short by almost sixty. I checked the math twice. I worked the hours. The register says the hours."

"Then somebody took it," Ava said.

"Nobody took it. It's all listed. Look, I'll send you mine."

So now the two stubs lay under the kitchen light, and their little printouts of deductions ran down the page like a grocery list of things Ava had never agreed to buy. On hers, under the net pay, were lines she read aloud slowly: income tax, then something called CPP, then something called EI. Federal income tax and provincial income tax, both there, both subtracted. She copied the numbers into her notebook and subtracted them herself, and they accounted for the whole fifty-nine, to the cent.

Priya's stub, though, did not match. The income tax lines were there, provincial and federal, but where Ava's said Canada Pension Plan, Priya's said something else entirely, a Quebec plan with a different name. And where Ava's said Employment Insurance, Priya's showed a parental insurance premium instead.

"We're missing something," Ava said when Priya called back at eight. "Your stub doesn't say EI. It says parental insurance."

"That's what it says," Priya said. "I didn't make it up. And it doesn't say Canada Pension Plan either, it says QPP. Quebec Pension Plan."

"So outside Quebec it's the Canada Pension Plan and EI, and in Quebec it's their own pension and their own parental insurance." Ava underlined this twice in her notebook. "That's the difference. It's not that your bakery is cheating you."

"My bakery," Priya said, "is run by a complete autocrat who counts the croissants every night, but no, apparently not a thief." She paused. "Does yours take the same amounts?"

Ava compared the percentages, line by line, and found they were close but not identical, though she couldn't tell, from one blurry printout, whether that was rates or wages or the fact that Priya worked Sundays at a premium. She said so, honestly, because pretending to certainty had never gone well for either of them.

The sales tax she worked out on her own, later, with a receipt from the laptop store where she'd gone just to look. The sticker price was eight ninety-nine, and when the clerk rang it up as a demonstration the total came to ten twenty and change, because the provincial and federal sales taxes were added at the till. She stood there doing the arithmetic on her phone and felt a small, cold clarity: the laptop was not nine hundred dollars. It was never going to be nine hundred dollars. Every price she had budgeted was a fiction until the tax landed on it, the same way her hourly wage had been a fiction until the deductions landed on that.

Her mother came home while Ava was still at the kitchen table with the receipts and the stubs and the notebook, and set down a bag of plums, and looked at the spread of paper for a long moment without touching it. "Doing your taxes?" she asked, half joking, because Ava had not yet filed anything in her life.

"Sort of. Learning them." Ava pulled the T4 slip she'd asked the grocery store for out of the folder, the summary of the year's wages and the deductions already taken, and set it beside the stubs. "Did you know that in Quebec they have a different pension plan? And parental insurance instead of EI?"

"I did not know that," her mother said, and pulled out the chair across from her, and took a plum, and sat down. "Show me."

Ava turned the notebook around so her underlines faced her mother, and slid Priya's blurry stub across the table beside her own, and put her finger on the two lines that did not match.

The festival on Beaumont Street had closed off three blocks, and by noon the smell of fried scallion cakes had desiccated in the heat until it was less a smell than a dust in the air. Maelie carried the red envelopes in her jacket pocket, four of them, folded flat, one for each of the younger cousins her mother had listed on the drive over. In her wallet she had the hundred and twenty dollars she had made over the summer tutoring calculus, and she had decided, without announcing it, that this year she would give from her own money rather than from the bills her mother handed out in the parking lot the way she had every year before.

She stood at the folding table near the lantern booth and counted. Twenty dollars for the twins, who were nine and would lose the money in a sock drawer anyway. Forty for Jun, who was thirteen and had asked her in August, in the tone of someone collecting data, whether red envelopes were essentially a transfer payment with a delay built in. She had laughed, then she had argued with him for an hour about whether tradition counted as an externality, some cost or benefit that landed on people who had never agreed to carry it. He was the only one in the family who talked to her like that, and forty felt like the right size for the conversation they had had.

Jun found her before she found him. He appeared at the table with a paper cup of shaved ice leaking pink syrup down his wrist, and he watched her slide the bills into the envelope one at a time.

"Stop," he said, when she reached the fourth twenty. "Not forty."

"Why not?"

"Four sounds like death. That's the whole rule. Any amount with a four in it." He said it the way he announced facts in debate rounds, flat and certain, and she stood holding the envelope half-full with a strange feeling, as though the money had changed weight in her hand.

She took out the fourth twenty and looked at it. Her mother was two booths away, haggling over a box of mandarins, and would not have said anything; her mother gave amounts with fours in them to the neighbors' kids and never seemed to think twice, or maybe never thought once. But Jun was standing there with syrup on his wrist, waiting, and the rule was the kind of thing that was either real or it wasn't, and if it was real then the number she had chosen for its generosity had been, all along, careless.

"Then what," she said. "Fifty?"

"Eight is better. Eight is the lucky one. Or just don't do forty." He shrugged, as if to say the system was arbitrary, which was his position on most systems, and also as if to say he would not be the one to walk around all evening holding money that meant death.

She put in the fourth twenty, then took it out again, then put in a fifth and a sixth, so the envelope held sixty. It was more than she had planned and less than she could defend, and she sealed it before she could do more arithmetic. Jun watched the whole operation and said nothing, which from him was a kind of respect.

They walked down the closed street together, past the lion dancers resting between performances, the lion's head tipped back against a folding chair, and past a church group handing out flyers about a different holiday two weeks away. She thought about her mother's parking-lot bills and Jun's flat certainty and the way her own position had shifted somewhere between the third twenty and the sixth, not because she had been convinced but because she had noticed that she wanted not to be the person who knew the rule and ignored it. That want was its own kind of information. Whether the rule was true, whether it was superstition or courtesy or something so endemic to the family that questioning it was like questioning the language they said it in, she still did not know, and she was unwilling to pretend the sixty dollars had settled anything.

"Here," she said, when they caught up with the cousins near the stage. She held out the envelope to Jun with both hands, because she had watched the aunts do it that way all her life and it seemed right. He took it with both hands too, formal, then ruined it immediately by shaking the envelope next to his ear.

"It's not a rattle," Maelie said.

"It's sixty dollars," Jun said. "I heard the denominations."

The twins had come to see, and the younger one was tugging at Maelie's sleeve, asking what was in hers, and the drums for the lion dancers were starting up again behind them.

The synagogue kitchen smelled of chicken soup and scorched candle wax, and Sienna stood at the counter with the Seder plate in both hands like something that might shatter if she thought too loudly about it. Rabbi Kessler had asked her in March, casually, the way adults ask for things they have already decided: her grandmother had led the family Seder for thirty-one years, and this year her grandmother was in a rehab facility in Scotch Plains relearning how to hold a fork. So it would be Sienna, at nineteen days old the youngest person ever entrusted with the plate, which held the shank bone and the egg and the charoset and the maror and the other symbols she had watched her grandmother name without ever once saying them herself.

Her first problem was horseradish. The sisterhood had requisitioned jars of it from the grocery on Springfield Avenue, whole jars, white and raw and brutal, and the amount terrified her. Her grandmother used to portion it out in doses the size of a pinky nail, and Sienna had spent the drive over trying to remember whether that was custom or mercy.

Her second problem was Marcus, her cousin's roommate from Rutgers, who had never been to a Seder in his life and had come anyway because Dana said the food was good and he had nowhere to go for the holiday. He sat at the far end of the table in the social hall looking like a man waiting for a dentist, and every time the Hebrew started his eyes went to the exits.

"Okay," Sienna said, standing, spoon raised, when they reached the point in the order of the service she had tabbed with a purple sticky note. "We're at maror. Everyone gets some horseradish."

Marcus raised his hand like they were still in lecture. "On purpose? You're handing out horseradish on purpose?"

"That's the maror," Sienna said. "Bitter herbs. We eat them to remember the bitterness of slavery in Egypt."

The whole table looked at her, waiting to see if she would go on, and she understood suddenly that her grandmother never had gone on, that the stopping was the point. She handed Marcus the jar.

He took a piece the size of a knuckle, which was his own error, and she watched his face travel through surprise, grief, and a brief flash of something bellicose before he grabbed the water glass Dana slid toward him. "Okay," he croaked. "That's a memory. I will never forget that."

"That's kind of the idea," Sienna said.

Later, while her Aunt Carol ladled soup and the little kids hunted for the hidden matzah under the folding chairs, Dana cornered her by the kitchen door. "You sounded like Grandma," Dana said. "Like exactly like her."

"She used to explain everything, though." Sienna pulled the Haggadah out from under a stack of napkins. "Forty minutes on every symbol. I have notes." She had, in fact, pages of them, plus a recording of last year's Seder her mother had made on her phone, and a highlighter-bright paperback called These Words Again that her intro-to-religion professor had recommended, a whole chapter on the hermeneutics of the Seder, on how the ritual was designed to make you ask rather than answer. She had read it twice on the train and underlined so much that the pages had gone soft.

"And you didn't use any of it."

"I used some of it. I just," Sienna said, and stopped, because the honest version was complicated. Her grandmother's way had been full, ornate, every story told twice. The book's way said the silence after the maror did the teaching by itself. Sienna had spent the whole week trying to choose between them and had ended up somewhere she couldn't quite name, doing her grandmother's ritual with her grandmother's silences left in, and she could not tell yet whether that was a synthesis or just a failure of nerve. "Next year in Jerusalem," she said, which was a dodge, and Dana laughed because they both knew it.

She slipped down the hall to the coatroom and called Scotch Plains. Her grandmother answered on the fourth ring, sounding papery but awake.

"Did you do the maror?" her grandmother asked, before Sienna said anything but hi.

"Small pieces. Like yours."

"Good. Small is right. Big pieces are showing off."

"Marcus took a big piece. A guest. I had to explain it fast." Sienna sat down on somebody's coat. "Was that okay? The short version?"

There was a pause long enough that Sienna heard the TV in the background, some game show wheel clicking. "Which part did you leave out?" her grandmother asked finally.

"The forty minutes."

Another pause. Then her grandmother made a sound that might have been a laugh or might have been the beginning of a cough. "Come Sunday," she said, "and bring the horseradish. I'll taste it and tell you if you got it right."

Sienna said she would, and hung up, and through the coatroom door she could hear Marcus in the social hall telling her little cousins, with great authority, to take a small piece, a very small piece, trust him on this.

James had circled the same eight bars four times and still could not decide where the first theme ended. The photocopy on the music stand was K. 283, the first movement, and Mrs. Okonkwo wanted the exposition marked off from the development and the recapitulation by Thursday. He had a pencil with a good eraser, which he had already used so much that the page wore a grey bloom wherever his brackets had been and been rubbed away.

The studio was on the second floor of her house, one room with an ascetic tidiness to it, a metronome, two chairs, nothing on the walls except a calendar from a piano tuner in Rotterdam. Mrs. Okonkwo believed in marking scores before playing them. "You wouldn't drive across a country without a map," she had said once, and James had pointed out that people did that all the time now, with their phones, and she had looked at him for a long moment and said, "Their phones have maps. That is my point."

He played the opening theme through, humming it under his breath. The trouble was that the theme did not simply stop. It dissolved. Somewhere around bar twenty the melody thinned into running figures, sixteenth notes chattering downward, and he could not find the seam where one thing became another. Was the first theme long or short? He had bracketed the ending in three places already and erased all three.

At home that night he exhumed an old recording from a box under his bed, a boxed set of the complete Mozart sonatas his grandmother had given him years ago, the discs still in their paper sleeves like something buried and half forgotten. He put on the first disc and lay on the floor with headphones and the score, listening with his finger on the page. He tried listening for the tune. Where the tune seemed to end, he put a bracket. Then the music went on doing something else for a long stretch, and the something else felt like it had somewhere to go.

He had a theory, which was that the theme ended when the tune ended, but the theory had a problem. After the tune stopped, the music got busier, not quieter, as though it were clearing its throat. And somewhere in that busy stretch, he was almost sure, the harmony slipped. He could not have said how he knew. It was like noticing that a room had got warmer without seeing anyone touch the thermostat.

The next afternoon his brother Dev was at the kitchen table doing economics homework, muttering about factories and rivers. "An externality," Dev said, not looking up, "is when the cost lands on somebody who wasn't in the deal. The factory makes the profit, the people downstream get the pollution." James, standing at the counter with his score, thought about the neighbours who heard his practising through the wall every evening, and then, unaccountably, about Mozart. He said, "Huh," and Dev said, "What," and James said, "Nothing," and went upstairs.

He listened again with headphones, and this time he followed the left hand instead of the right. The bass stepped down, and down again, and then the music arrived somewhere it had not been before, a place that felt like a different room in the same house. When the second tune finally appeared, it sat comfortably in that new place. He found the spot where the arrival happened, and then he worked backwards, asking where the leaving had started, and the leaving seemed to start exactly where the tune stopped and the chattering began.

He texted his friend Priya, who was doing the same assignment for a different teacher. Priya said she had drawn her first-theme bracket through bar 41 because her teacher liked long themes. James typed, then deleted, then typed: try finding where it changes key. The part that gets busy. Priya sent back a question mark, so he called her.

"Okay," he said, phone wedged against his shoulder, score on the desk. "The busy part, the not-very-tuneful part, right after the first tune. That's the transition. Or the bridge. It's the passage in the exposition that moves from the home key to the second key." There was a pause while Priya, presumably, hunted for her pencil. "Mine's all scales," she said. "Like it's showing off and pretending to be a conversation." "Exactly," James said. "It doesn't want to be a tune. It wants to get somewhere."

On Thursday Mrs. Okonkwo took his marked score and read it in silence for longer than felt comfortable. Her pencil hovered over his bracket at the end of the first theme. "And why here?" she asked. James said it was where the tune stopped and the busy passage began, the one that shifted from the home key toward the second key, and she nodded once, which from her was applause. Then she turned to his recapitulation bracket and tapped it. "And here? Same reasoning?" He had marked the recapitulation the way he had because the tune came back and he wanted to be finished. He looked at the place she was tapping and realised he had not checked whether the busy passage there changed key or not, and if it did not, then where exactly had he drawn the line, and why.

"Actually," he said, "I'm not sure that one's right."

"Good," said Mrs. Okonkwo, and put the score back on the stand. She sat down at the piano and played his exposition bracket to the end of the first theme, then lifted her hands entirely, and the silence after the tune stopped was so complete that James could hear the Rotterdam calendar page ticking in the draft from the window.

Tristan had told himself he would be calm about the interview, and for most of the walk to Halvorsen's Hardware he believed he had been calm, though his hands were damp by the time he pushed through the glass door and the bell rang above him. Mr. Halvorsen was at the register, ringing up a coil of copper wire, and he only glanced up and said, "Tristan, right? You're the one who called Tuesday." Tristan said yes, and Mr. Halvorsen said, "Forklift guy quit, so I need someone on Saturdays and two evenings. Can you start Friday? I mean it, Friday, because inventory's due and I'll be dead by the weekend if I'm counting bolts alone."

That was how the job began, with a deadline instead of a handshake. Tristan spent Thursday night reading a laminated sheet of aisle codes until the numbers started to calcify in his head, so that even lying in the dark he was murmuring "six, fasteners; seven, adhesives," and he told himself this was preparation, not nerves. He was certain he had told his mother the pay rate was twelve dollars an hour. He was so certain that when she asked him over breakfast he said, "Twelve, obviously, why would I not remember twelve," in the tone of someone who has not quite verified it.

His first two shifts were shelving and hauling and learning that customers who say "just the small ones" mean four different sizes. On Friday night, his third shift, Mr. Halvorsen handed him a check and said the payroll lady needed his hiring form back before Monday or the whole cycle would slip. Tristan looked at the number on the check and his stomach dropped. It was smaller than it should have been. He did the arithmetic twice while restocking washers, his lips moving, and it kept coming out wrong, and he thought, I was lied to, or I misremembered, and the second possibility was the unbearable one, because he had already spent the money in his head on a speaker he did not need.

"Mr. Halvorsen," he said, approaching the register at closing, "I worked fourteen hours. At twelve an hour that's a hundred sixty-eight. This is less." He held the check out flat, like evidence. Mr. Halvoren took his time counting out the drawer before he answered, and in that silence Tristan's certainty curdled into dread, because he remembered, suddenly and completely, that the number in the interview had been eleven fifty, and he had upgraded it himself, quietly, on the walk home.

"Nobody skimmed you," Mr. Halvorsen said. "There's withholding. Social Security takes its cut." He tapped the pay stub attached to the check. Tristan turned the stub toward the light. There it was, a line labeled Social Security, and a smaller line of figures beside it. He read them in the fluorescent hush while Mr. Halvorsen locked the front door and the bell gave one last ring. "It's 6.2 percent," Mr. Halvorsen said, halfway to the back. "Of your wages. Only up to a yearly wage limit, so if you somehow got rich off me, it would stop somewhere. You won't, but that's the rule." He said it the way a man says something he has explained a hundred times to a hundred sixteen-year-olds, without malice, and disappeared into the stockroom.

Tristan stood at the register with the stub and did the arithmetic a third time, slowly now, the way the tense moments demanded. Six point two percent of eleven fifty, times fourteen hours, plus the other deductions he did not yet have names for, and the check's number resolved into sense. It was not theft. It was the ordinary machinery of a paycheck, which he had never seen before because he had never had one, and which had been running the whole time in the dark.

He walked home under the streetlights holding two ideas that refused to merge cleanly. His father called taxes the price of living in a society, and said anyone who griped about them was a detractor of things he relied on every day. His uncle called withholding a profligate habit, the government spending your money before you ever touched it. Both of them were certain. Tristan, doing the last of the math on his phone outside his building, found he could not be certain in either direction. He owed the machine something he would never see returned in any recognizable form, and he could not say whether that was fair, only that it was the deal, and that he had signed it the moment he wanted the money more than he wanted the certainty.

His mother was still up, waiting with the form. He filled in the blanks at the kitchen table, and she asked how it went. "It's less than I thought," he said, and then, before she could frown, "but now I know why." He signed his name in the box, and the pen skipped once on the last letter.

Jasmine had acclimated to the smell of the bakery by her second week, yeast and burnt sugar, but she had not acclimated to closing alone. The manager, Denny, had left at eight for a dentist appointment, and the handwritten list taped above the register said only, "Count twice. Call me." At 9:40 she counted the drawer the first time and got a number that made her check the ceiling for a prank. She was short forty-one dollars and seventeen cents.

She counted again, slower, laying the twenties in a fan across the counter the way Denny did. Same total. She counted the debit receipts, the credit slips, the voided orders, the two bags of day-old bread the shelter pickup had signed for. Forty-one dollars and seventeen cents, an amount so specific it had to mean something. It sat there under the fluorescents like a tectonic shift in a place she had thought was flat.

The problem was that she needed this job. Her mother had said, over the application forms in March, that a first paycheque was a small education in itself, and her mother had been right in a way neither of them had predicted. The first cheque had come with a pay stub that read like a foreign document: gross pay, then lines subtracting income tax, then CPP, then EI, until the net pay at the bottom was a smaller, chastened number. Jasmine had taped the stub inside her binder for reasons she couldn't fully explain, except that the distance between the top line and the bottom line felt like information about the adult world that adults themselves never mentioned. She had looked up the deduction names at the library and understood roughly a third of it, which was a third more than her friend Priya, whose entire financial theory was that taxes were theft.

She was still standing over the drawer when her phone buzzed. Priya, from the group chat, had posted a photograph of a receipt from a coffee shop in London, where her cousin was travelling, next to a receipt from the bakery where Jasmine worked. "Why does their receipt not show tax," Priya wrote. "Is London a scam or are we."

Jasmine looked at the two images. The bakery receipt showed her subtotal, then HST added below it, then the total. The London receipt showed only the price of the flat white and a cake, no separate tax line at all. She sat down on the stool behind the counter and searched on her phone with the slow patience of someone avoiding a worse task. She found a government page, then a forum, then her cousin's own travel blog, and piece by piece the thing assembled itself. In the United Kingdom the sales tax was called VAT, and unlike her receipt at home, it was built into the prices people saw; the standard rate had been twenty percent since the fourth of January, 2011, which meant Priya's cousin had paid it, invisibly, on the cake. "It's called VAT," Jasmine typed back, "and it's already inside the price." She added the date, because Priya would argue otherwise, and Priya did, and Jasmine pasted the link and went back to the drawer.

Forty-one seventeen. She thought about arbitrage, a word from a documentary she'd watched about currency traders, about gaps between two systems that someone could exploit. If a customer had paid with a large bill and she'd made change wrong, the gap would be between what was owed and what was given. She reconstructed the night order by order from the till tape, and stopped at 7:52. Two coffees, a box of tarts, a loaf. Cash, fifty-dollar bill. She remembered the man, because he'd asked whether the prices on the chalkboard included tax, and she'd said yes out of instinct, and he'd said, "Good, like London," and she hadn't known what he meant until tonight.

She found the error in the tape. The register had the order as $31.85, tax included. She had punched in the pre-tax subtotal and then tax again, so the machine believed it was owed more than the man had paid, and she had handed him change for the inflated figure. He had walked out with the extra money folded in his palm, unbothered, while she smiled at the door. She read the arithmetic three times, hoping it would rearrange itself.

There was still the question of what to do. Forty-one seventeen out of a paycheque whose net was already a bruised thing. Denny had a rule about shortages, announced once with his hand flat on the counter: they come out of the shift that caused them. She got her jacket to leave a note confessing everything, and under the till drawer she found an envelope she had missed, Denny's handwriting on the front. "Took float cash for the bank run before dentist. Minus it from the count. Don't panic, I always tell you this and you always forget."

She read it twice, then laughed once, quietly, in the empty bakery. The man from 7:52 had still walked out with money that wasn't his, and Denny's note had already subtracted exactly what she'd calculated the loss to be, forty-one seventeen, before she had ever found her own error. She put the envelope back, closed the drawer, and texted Priya a photograph of the empty storefront with the lights half down. "I solved two tax mysteries tonight," she wrote, "and I'm only getting paid for one."

The community kitchen on Delancey Street smelled of bleach and cinnamon at once, which Cohen decided was the smell of other people's good intentions. He had the place to himself for two hours on Thursday nights, a perk of his mother's volunteer shift that nobody had asked him about, and tonight he was making dinner for the whole family because his mother had texted that morning: "Working double. Dad's at the hospital with Grandma. You're cooking, chicken thighs in the fridge, don't burn the apartment down." She signed it with a thumbs-up, which he read as either trust or surrender.

He laid the thighs on the counter and turned on the tap, holding the first one under cold water the way his grandmother had done every Sunday of his childhood, working her thumbs over the skin like she was absolving it. He was reaching for the second when his sister Nadia appeared in the doorway, still wearing her debate team lanyard.

"Stop. What are you doing."

"Washing it. Like Grandma."

"Don't. The CDC says not to wash raw chicken." She dropped her bag on a stool. "The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and the surfaces around it."

Cohen kept his hand under the tap a moment longer, water running pale over the skin, then shut it off. "Grandma did it her whole life."

"Grandma also smoked for thirty years. Turn the tap off all the way."

He dried the thigh on a paper towel, annoyed at how quickly he'd obeyed, and annoyed at the small wet halo already drying on the stainless steel. He wiped it down with the disinfectant spray the kitchen kept stocked, twice, feeling foolish both times.

"Since when do you quote the CDC?"

"Since microbiology unit." She pulled an onion toward her and began peeling it, which was her way of admitting she intended to stay. "Ms. Okafor showed us a video. Water hits the chicken and the spray goes everywhere. You can't see it, but it lands on the counter, the faucet, whatever's in the sink."

"So Grandma was poisoning us every Sunday?"

"I'm not saying that." Nadia's knife work was faster than his; she'd always been the precise one, a virtuoso with anything edged, while Cohen thought of himself as the improviser, the one who could taste a sauce and know what it wanted. "I'm saying she didn't know, and now we do, and knowing is only useful if you change what you do."

He salted the chicken while he thought about that. His grandmother had a theory of cooking that was also a theory of people: you cleaned what you could see, you trusted what you couldn't, and you didn't let a government pamphlet tell you how to touch your own food. She'd have said Nadia was confusing caution with wisdom. And yet the thing in Nadia's video was invisible and real, bacteria riding droplets across a counter, and Grandma's defense against it had been nothing but habit. Maybe the two of them were both right about different things, and the chicken didn't care which grandmother he believed.

He set the thighs skin-down in a pan that was almost hot enough, and the hiss came up loud and immediate, the kitchen filling with the smell of browning fat. Nadia diced the onion smaller than he would have, fine and even. "Grandma would say you're sublimating your anxiety into knife work," he said.

"Grandma used that word wrong her whole life too." But she almost smiled.

He built the rest of it without a recipe, because that was the part he was good at: paprika, the lemon going soft and friable in his hand from sitting too long in the fridge, its rind giving way under his thumb. Rice in the big pot. He tasted, added, tasted again. He kept thinking about the tap water, how something could spread exactly because you were trying to clean it, and how that felt true about more than chicken, and how he couldn't quite say what. He decided he didn't have to decide tonight. He would cook the way the evidence said and remember Grandma's hands anyway, and if those two things sat uneasily together, well, that was what a counter was for.

When the thighs came out of the pan, crackling and dark at the edges, he plated four servings even though it was just him and Nadia tonight, one for his mother to find in the microwave after her double, one for his father at the hospital. Nadia stole a piece of skin off the first plate, which was as close to praise as she got.

His phone buzzed against the counter. His mother: "Grandma's asking if you're making her chicken. Tell her yes. Tell her you're making it just like hers."

Nadia read it over his shoulder and looked at him. Cohen typed back, "I'm making it mine. She'll like it," and put the phone face-down next to the stove, and carried the plates to the table.

The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and overheated laptops, and Sadie had been standing behind her poster for two hours before the second judge arrived. Her project was a set of sealed tubes in a warming bath, a trick she had borrowed from her chemistry teacher's cabinet and half rebuilt on her own time. The poster said Equilibrium Under Stress, which she now regretted, because the title invited exactly the questions she was least sure she could answer.

"Walk me through it," the judge said. He was young, maybe a graduate student, with a lanyard that said MARCUS and a pen he didn't use.

She lifted the first tube. The gas inside was pale, almost colorless. "It's at equilibrium," she said. "Both directions of the reaction are happening at the same rate, so nothing appears to change. And then I heat it." She lowered the tube into the bath, held it, and lifted it out again. The gas had gone brown, deepening at the top like tea steeping.

"So heating made more of the brown stuff."

"Made the equilibrium shift toward it." She heard her own hedge and pressed on. "The system pushes back. When you disturb a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change. That's Le Chatelier's principle." The line came out flat, recited, and Marcus looked at her the way people look at a locked door.

"Partly," he repeated. "Not completely."

"Right. It can't undo the change. It just leans against it."

He asked her what would happen if she cooled the tube instead, and she said it should lean the other way, back toward the colorless gas, and he said should, and she said yes, should, and he wrote nothing and moved on to the robotics table. She stood there holding the warm tube, feeling that she had defended a position she wasn't sure she owned.

At 11:40 her phone buzzed against the folding table. A text from Theo, who was thirteen and had commandeered her second set of tubes for a kitchen-table experiment while their mother was at work.

I sealed two tubes like yours. Gonna heat one on the stove. Tell me what happens before I do it so we can check.

She typed: If you heat it the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the change. So toward the brown gas. Tube should get darker.

how do you know it doesn't just all turn brown

She stared at that. She didn't know, exactly. Because partly, she typed. It leans, it doesn't flip. Then, before he could ask the next question: Do it and tell me what you see. Take a picture.

Her mother had a rule about the stove, which Theo was violating, and Sadie had a rule about doing her brother's thinking for him, which she was also violating, and she stood in the gymnasium between these two small betrayals while a girl from the next table asked to borrow her stopwatch.

The afternoon had its own arithmetic. Sadie had built the project believing that prediction was the whole point of science, that knowing a principle meant owning the future. Marcus's questions had sensitized her to something else: the difference between reciting a rule and being able to say where it stopped. Her grandfather, a retired engineer, had called theories like this obsolescent furniture, ideas you kept in the attic because they worked well enough for daily life even if nobody built houses that way anymore. She had liked the phrase without understanding it. Now she wondered whether leaning was a real description or a metaphor that had hardened into one.

Theo's picture arrived at 12:15. The tube over the burner had gone the exact brown of hers, richer at the top, and beneath it he had written, you were right, it only partly counteracted, and then a second message: the other tube I put in the freezer went almost clear. does it work both ways?

She typed yes and then deleted it, because that was the recitation again, the reflexive answer, and she had watched enough judges today to know the difference between a claim and a demonstration. Wait twenty minutes and look again, she sent instead. Tell me if it stays clear.

While she waited she cooled her own tube in the ice bath she had ignored all day, and the brown thinned, and she felt the small vertigo of watching a prediction hold. A woman with a clipboard came by and asked whether the reaction ever truly stopped, and Sadie said no, both directions kept going, they just balanced, and the woman said that sounded like marriage, and Sadie laughed before she could stop herself.

Theo's next message came at 12:40. still clear. does cold count as a disturbance or is it just nothing happening

She read it three times. It was the question Marcus had circled without asking, the one she had answered with should, and she understood now that she could hold two things at once: the principle worked, it had worked twice today in two kitchens, and still she could not say why cold counted as a disturbance rather than an absence, only that the system responded to it as one. That was not a failure of the principle. It was the edge of what she knew about it.

She wrote back: Cold counts. It shifts to lean against that too. Then, because he was thirteen and deserved the whole truth: I don't know exactly why it counts. Ask me again when I'm in college.

Marcus came back at two o'clock with a ribbon in his hand, small and green, third place, and asked if she had figured out the cooling yet. She lifted the clear tube out of the ice and held it up between them.

"It leans," she said. "That's all I can tell you for sure."

The smell hit Alex before the door did: latkes frying in oil, onion and potato burned to the edge of black the way his grandmother liked, the way nobody else in the family could bear. Inside, the apartment had already filled, cousins in the kitchen arguing about whose turn it was to man the skillet, his mother by the window with a glass of wine she was nursing rather than drinking. It was the fourth night of Hanukkah, and the menorah waited on the sideboard, silver gone dull where nobody had polished it since last winter.

Alex had offered to set it up. That was the whole of his plan, small and deliberate: do one thing tonight that wasn't just eating and leaving. He'd spent the fall semester reading philosophy for a required course and finding, to his surprise, that the arguments he liked best were the ones his grandmother had been performing in this kitchen since he was small. His mother, meanwhile, had stopped coming to these nights years ago and only resumed when Alex asked, which he had, awkwardly, over text. He wanted to stand somewhere between them without pretending either one was wrong.

He carried the box of candles to the sideboard and lifted the lid. His grandmother's menorah had nine branches, he noticed now for the first time, though he could not have said he'd ever counted. Eight of them in a row, and one set apart, slightly higher. He began setting candles into the holders, thinking about his ethics paper, thinking about the latkes, thinking about the girl from his seminar who had told him that ritual was either everything or nothing. When he looked down, he had placed six candles and could not remember whether he'd meant to place four.

"You're building a bonfire," his cousin Dani said over his shoulder, laughing. He was eleven and took a proprietary interest in the menorah, the way kids take an interest in whatever they are newly allowed to touch. "It's the fourth night. Four."

"I knew that," Alex said, and didn't, entirely. He pulled two candles free and set them back in the box, then frowned at the row: four candles in the low holders, and the tall holder at the end still empty. "What's the extra one for? There's a ninth."

Dani looked at him with frank disappointment. "The shamash," he said, as if naming a family member. "The helper candle. You use it to light the others. And you're supposed to put one more in each night." He plucked a candle from the box and set it in the tall holder with a surgeon's care, then smoothed its wick between two fingers, as if to burnish the whole arrangement into correctness.

Alex stood with his hand still hovering over the holder, absorbing it. Eight branches for the eight nights, one more each night, and a ninth that existed only to give its fire away. Something in him turned the shape of it over. The shamash wasn't part of the count; it was what made the counting visible. His philosophy professor had spent a week on means and ends, and here was the whole argument standing on his grandmother's sideboard in beeswax. He thought of his mother by the window, who believed the candles were lovely and meant nothing, and of the seminar girl, who believed they were meaningless unless they meant everything, and found that he could hold both and still strike a match.

"Grandma," he called toward the kitchen, "who's lighting tonight?"

She came out wiping her hands on a dish towel, and there was a small negotiation, because Dani claimed the right by seniority of enthusiasm, and Alex claimed it by three months of homesickness, and their grandmother ruled in favor of Alex on the grounds that he'd set it up wrong and could therefore be trusted to fix it. His mother drifted over from the window. The window's cold light and the kitchen's warm one met at the sideboard, and for a moment everyone was in the same place, an unusual consonance in a family that conducted most of its disagreements from separate rooms.

He lit the shamash first, the match flaring and then steadying, its small sulfur smell folding into the oil and onion. Four flames, then, one after another, each tipped from the helper candle's fire, and he said the blessings in a voice that surprised him by not shaking. His pronunciation was worse than Dani's. His grandmother closed her eyes, and his mother, who knew no Hebrew at all, stood quietly with her hands wrapped around her glass and watched the candles with an expression Alex couldn't read and didn't try to. He didn't know what he believed, exactly, and suspected he wouldn't for years; he knew only that he had wanted to be the one holding the fire, and that he was.

"Same time tomorrow?" his mother said, under the noise of the cousins heading back to the latkes. "Fifth night. Five candles."

"Five plus the shamash," Alex said.

She smiled at him over the rim of her glass. "So you were paying attention."

Dominic spread the index cards across his grandfather's kitchen table, twenty-two of them, each with a date in blue pen and an event below it in pencil so he could rearrange his mind without erasing history. The assignment was supposed to be simple: a timeline of the Cold War's origins, due Thursday. The problem was the first card. Every timeline needed a beginning, and Dominic had two candidates and no way to choose.

"Your grandmother keeps the good tea in the cupboard above the stove," his grandfather said, setting down a mug of something that smelled like burnt hay. "What's all this?"

"The Cold War. I have to mark where it started." Dominic tapped the February 1946 card. "Kennan's Long Telegram. That's when an American diplomat in Moscow basically said the Soviets were expansionist and the US had to contain them. My textbook ascribes the whole containment strategy to it."

His grandfather pulled out a chair and sat, which Dominic understood as a commitment of at least forty minutes. "And the other card?"

"March 1947." Dominic slid it forward. "The Truman Doctrine. He announced that the US would support countries resisting communist pressure, starting with aid to Greece and Turkey."

"Four hundred million dollars, I seem to recall, though don't quote me."

"I won't. That's not on my card." Dominic flattened a card that had curled. "So which is it? A telegram no one outside the government read, or a public promise with money behind it?"

His grandfather drank his terrible tea and said nothing for a while, which was his way of saying that the question was better than Dominic knew. Down the hall, Dominic's mother was arguing with the printer, which had jammed on her boarding pass for the third time. Somewhere in the argument the word "autocrat" surfaced, aimed at the machine, and Dominic laughed before he could stop himself.

At school on Monday the question got worse. Mr. Reyes had divided the class into pairs and given each pair two historians' explanations to weigh against the evidence, and Dominic's partner, Priya, had come in with both articles annotated in three colors of highlighter. "Post-revisionist," she said, tapping the first. "He argues the US and the USSR each ascribed hostile motives to the other that neither fully held. It was mutual misreading, not one villain." She tapped the second. "This one says the Soviets really were consolidating a sphere, and the American response was predictable, maybe even necessary."

"So where does my start date fit?" Dominic laid the cards out on the desk between them. "If the Long Telegram is the start, then the war begins with a perception, an American official deciding the Soviets were dangerous. That supports the misreading guy. If the Truman Doctrine is the start, it begins with an actual commitment, a real promise with Greece and Turkey attached."

Priya frowned at the cards. "Couldn't you argue the telegram is just a private opinion and the doctrine is the first policy? Like, an opinion isn't a war."

"But the historian I read says the telegram shaped everything that came after. If ideas move history, then the perception is the start." Dominic turned the March 1947 card over and back. "The problem is I can't prove what moved Truman. Maybe he'd already decided, and the telegram just gave him language. Or maybe the language made the decision. The evidence looks the same either way."

They worked through lunch, Priya reading passages aloud while Dominic wrote and crossed out. By the end he had a paragraph he half believed: the Long Telegram supplied the interpretation, the Truman Doctrine converted it into commitment, and neither alone was the start, the way a match isn't a fire and a fire isn't a match. But he wrote in the margin, in pencil, that he couldn't show the telegram actually caused the doctrine, only that it came first. Priya read the margin note and said, "He'll dock you points for hedging."

"He can dock me," Dominic said. "I'm not going to pretend the evidence is cleaner than it is." It came out more loudly than he intended, and the boy at the next table looked over, and Dominic felt his ears go warm. Some kinds of honesty sounded like arguments even when they weren't.

Thursday he handed in the timeline with the March 1947 card placed first, a small penciled star next to the telegram, and the hedge left in. That evening his grandfather called. "I found my old textbook in the attic," he said. "1961 edition. You'll want to see the start date it gives."

Dominic felt the whole careful structure of his week tilt. "Which one is it?"

"Neither," his grandfather said, and there was a smile in his voice. "It starts in 1917. They went all the way back to the Bolshevik Revolution. There's a whole chapter before your telegram even shows up."

The computer lab smelled of floor wax and overheated monitors, and Madison had forty minutes before the bell. She typed the class the way the worksheet showed it, a BankAccount with a private double balance and a private String owner, then wrote the getters, getBalance and getOwner, each one returning its field. The worksheet's last step was to write a constructor that set both fields, instantiate two accounts in the test class, and print them. She had done the readings the night before, or most of them, scrolling on her phone with one thumb while the textbook lay open and unread on her desk. Now that neglect had a cost, and the cost was due at the end of the period.

"CheckCompile.java:14: error: invalid method declaration; return type required." She read the message three times. Line fourteen was her constructor, public void BankAccount(double startBalance, String name). She highlighted the line, deleted the word void, retyped it, deleted it again. Around her, keyboards clattered. Mr. Ferreira sat at the front desk grading quizzes and had announced, when asked about errors, that the compiler was the real teacher today.

"Yours won't run either?" Desmond leaned over from the next station, chair wheels squeaking. He was the one who had finished the Python unit early and then acted bored for three weeks.

"Mine compiles fine," Madison said. "It just prints zeros. My balance comes out zero no matter what I pass in." She showed him the output: 0.0, null. It was the account she had constructed with two hundred dollars and her own name, and it had arrived in the world empty, like a wallet someone else had already picked clean. "The constructor just doesn't run."

"Did you return anything from it?"

"No. It's a constructor, it's not supposed to." She wasn't sure she believed her own sentence. She wrote a print statement inside the constructor braces and ran the test again. Nothing printed. The method sat there like a door painted on a wall.

Desmond pulled his chair closer and read her code sideways. "You wrote void in front of it."

"So? Every method has a return type."

"Look at the worksheet example." He flipped the page. The sample constructor had no return type at all, not even void, and suddenly Madison understood with a visceral certainty that made her ears go hot: by writing void, she had turned her constructor into an ordinary method, a method that happened to share the class's name and that nothing ever called. It sat in the file like an unused appliance. The real constructor, the one Java would actually run, was the invisible default one the compiler quietly supplied, the one that set everything to zero. That was why her account held 0.0 and null. Her two hundred dollars hadn't been lost; they had never been deposited.

She deleted the void and ran it. "MADISON 200.0" printed in the console, and then "DESMOND 500.0," because he had typed himself into her test file while she wasn't looking. She should have felt triumph, and partly did, but something else nagged at her. All semester she had treated programming as a matter of following shapes, copying the silhouette of code from examples and trusting the outline to hold. The error message had told her the shape was wrong without telling her why, and only by holding two things side by side, her line and the worksheet's line, had she seen the difference. She recalibrated, or tried to: less copying, more reading of what was actually there. Though she had to admit, to herself if not out loud, that she still couldn't say why the language had been designed that way, only that it was.

Desmond, for his part, watched her fix it and felt his own confidence wobble. He had assumed the bug was hers, some careless typo, and had enjoyed for about ninety seconds the prospect of explaining it to her. Now he understood that she had found the answer herself by putting a print statement where he would never have thought to put one, inside a method that wasn't running, to prove it wasn't running. That was a different kind of thinking than his, and he wasn't sure it was worse. He scrolled up through his own file, double-checking his constructors for a void he'd suddenly become unsure about.

"Wait," he said. "So the constructor has the same name as the class, and no return type, not even void."

"Not even void," Madison said. "That's the whole trap." She added a third account to the test, this one for their friend Priya with a balance of twelve dollars, ran it, and watched all three names line up in the console with their balances beside them.

Priya leaned across the aisle, screen light on her face. "Can I copy your fix?"

"Copy the idea," Madison said, and turned her monitor toward her. "Find your own void."

Justin had been playing clarinet for six weeks, and Mrs. Okafor's studio still smelled to him like reeds and old coffee, a smell he had begun to think of as the smell of being bad at something in public. Today she had propped her phone on the music stand with a tuner app open, a green needle wobbling on a gray dial.

"Play your A," she said. "Concert A. Anchor yourself there before we go anywhere."

He played it. The needle sagged left. "Four thirty-eight," she said, tapping the screen where the number sat below the dial. "The standard is four forty. You're flat by a breath."

That part he understood. What he did not understand came five minutes later, when she had him slur up an octave. He watched the number out of the corner of his eye, mostly because watching the needle felt less embarrassing than watching her face, and the digits jumped from 440 to 880. He stopped mid-note.

"Did you see that?" he asked.

"See what?"

"The number doubled. Exactly. I played the same letter, one octave up, and it went four forty to eight eighty. That's not a coincidence, right? That's twice."

Mrs. Okafor folded her arms, which was what she did instead of smiling, because smiling was apparently a concession she made rarely and on her own terms. "What do you think?"

"I think somebody designed it that way. Like the notes are a system, not just, I don't know, vibes."

"Somebody designed it that way," she agreed, "but not recently, and not by committee. Play it again and watch."

He played it again. 440, then 880, clean as arithmetic. His father, an engineer, had a word for people who trusted vibes over systems, and it was not a kind word; his mother, a painter, had roughly the same word for people who trusted systems over vibes. Justin had spent sixteen years caught between two households that each considered the other's certainty a kind of blindness, and he had lately begun to suspect that both of them were ideologues of one stripe or another, his father worshiping the number, his mother worshiping the slippage around it. The doubling felt like evidence for a third position he could not yet name: the world had structure in it, and the structure was beautiful, and neither of his parents owned it.

"Your octave is narrow," Mrs. Okafor said. "You're thinking your way up instead of hearing your way up. The clarinet doesn't care what you've concluded."

"That's harsh."

"That's Tuesday." She took the phone off the stand and slid it into her cardigan pocket, and the subtext of the gesture was unmistakable, so unmistakable that she let it be unmistakable: the numbers had told him something true, and now the numbers were leaving the room. "Play the two As again. No screen. Tell me when the upper one is true."

He played the low A, then reached upward and overshot, thin and sharp, the sound of someone trying too hard to be right. He tried again, undershot, went flat, and heard his own frustration begin to adumbrate the note itself, darkening the tone before it even left the horn. He stopped, breathed, and thought: 880. Not as a rule to obey but as a place to land. He played the low A, let it settle, and then let the octave happen rather than performing it.

"Better," she said. "Nearly."

"Nearly is worse than no," Justin said, which was a thing his father said, and he heard himself say it, and he hated how insouciant it had sounded coming out of him, glib, like wisdom he had shoplifted.

"Nearly is the whole job," Mrs. Okafor said. "Also, your father called me."

He froze with the clarinet still at his lip. "About what?"

"He wants to know if you're progressing at an acceptable rate. I told him you ask good questions and play narrow octaves."

"You told him that?"

"I told him you'd be fine by winter," she said, taking the phone back out of her pocket and setting it on the stand, screen dark this time, just a black rectangle, a promise of verification held in reserve. "Winter is a guess, of course. I've been wrong before, and the doubling of frequencies won't save you from rolling your fingers late. But you found the eight eighty on your own, and you found it by watching instead of by asking, and that's worth more than my guess."
