Justin looked at the dark screen, then at the window, where a delivery truck was backing into the alley with its beeper going, two tones, high and low, over and over.

"Play your A," Mrs. Okafor said. "We'll take winter when it comes."

The copper sulfate solution had been sitting on the windowsill since Tuesday, and by Friday the crystals at the bottom of the jar looked like something a very small dragon had hoarded and then abandoned. Logan set the jar on the kitchen table next to the scale, a borrowed thing from the chemistry room that his teacher had handed over with the expression of a man lending out a kidney.

The science fair was in nine days. His board was half-finished in the garage, its title slightly too grandiose for what had actually occurred: "Controlled Growth of Copper Sulfate Pentahydrate Crystals." Controlled was generous. So far the crystals had grown wherever they pleased and in shapes resembling gravel.

His mother was at the stove, something with cabbage that would ferment if nobody ate it soon, a smell that was already lobbying for attention. "Did you weigh them dry?" she asked, without turning around.

"That's what I'm doing." He fished the largest crystal out with tweezers, blotted it on a paper towel, and set it on the scale. The display blinked and settled: 4.1 grams. He wrote it in his notebook, then wrote it again in neater handwriting, as if the second version might be more cooperative.

The problem was the paper towel. Or possibly the crystal. He had started, in theory, with a weighed amount of copper sulfate, dissolved in water he had measured twice, and the whole point of the project was to show what you could predict. He had done the stoichiometry at the kitchen table three nights running: grams of reactant divided by molar mass to get moles, moles carried across the balanced equation, moles converted back to grams of product. Twenty-five grams of copper sulfate pentahydrate, molar mass 249.7, should have given him a theoretical yield of product he'd calculated to the second decimal place. He turned to that page now. 6.3 grams of crystal, if everything went perfectly.

He weighed the crystal again. Still 4.1. He weighed the smaller fragments one at a time, tong-like with the tweezers, adding each mass to the running total, and the total came to 4.7 grams, which was not 6.3 grams and did not seem interested in becoming 6.3 grams.

His sister Delia came in, opened the fridge, and evaluated its contents with the disappointment of a returning customer. "You look like the crystals died."

"They didn't die. They underperformed." He showed her the page, the careful chain of conversions, the theoretical yield circled twice. "I did the math right. I checked it against the example in the book. The moles are the moles."

"So the math's right and the crystals are wrong."

"That's not how chemistry works. Or it's exactly how chemistry works. I can't tell yet." He pulled the calculator toward him and, half to himself, divided the actual mass by the theoretical yield. 4.7 divided by 6.3. He multiplied by 100 and stared at the number: about seventy-five percent.

"What's that?" Delia asked, leaning over his shoulder with a piece of cheese she had found somewhere.

"Percent yield," he said. "Actual mass of product divided by the theoretical yield, times a hundred."

"So you got a seventy-five."

"Seventy-five percent. Which means a quarter of my copper is somewhere it shouldn't be." He looked at the jar, at the blue scum ringing the waterline where crystals had nucleated on the glass instead of on his seed crystal, at the paper towel still faintly damp and probably faintly blue. Some of the missing mass was on the towel. Some was on the jar. Some had probably stayed dissolved in the water he'd poured off, because decanting was a word he'd used confidently at the time and understood less now.

His mother set a bowl of the cabbage stuff in front of him and stayed leaning against the counter, arms folded, watching him the way she watched weather. "Is that bad? The seventy-five."

"It depends on who you ask." He was beginning to see it two ways at once, and neither way was wrong. One version of the project said: here is a failure, the crystals disobeyed, hide the discrepancy and report the pretty number. The other version said: here is a method, the math held, the world added its own margin, and a seventy-five percent yield was itself a result, maybe the honest one, maybe even the interesting one. What he couldn't yet say was how much of the missing twenty-five percent was sloppy technique and how much was just how the universe did business, and he suspected the answer was both, inseparably.

He took the pen and wrote the number on the back of his hand so he wouldn't lose it. Then he carried the jar to the sink, tipped out the pale blue water, and held the glass up to the window so the light caught the ragged little city of crystals clinging to the side.

"Yours?" Delia asked.

"Mine," he said. "All 4.7 grams of them."

The restaurant had been closed to the public since four, and by six the long tables were full of everyone from Mathis's graduating class who bothered to come. His uncle had rented the back room for the occasion, and the waiters moved between the tables with trays of sparkling cider because most of them were still eighteen, still months from anything legal. Mathis sat between his mother and a girl named Priya who had beaten him in every essay contest since tenth grade, and he kept looking at the empty chairs near the far end, where the Fernando brothers should have been.

He had made a list, actually, folded into his jacket pocket, of everyone who had started ninth grade with him. It began as a joke, something cerebral he'd intended to read aloud, a little archive of homeroom memories. But when he counted the names against the faces in the room, the joke stopped working. He found Priya refilling her glass at the drink table and asked her, quietly, about the Fernandos.

"Rafa's cousin said he's working at the distribution center off Route 9," she said. "Tomas went back to Oaxaca in junior year. You knew that." She said it without cruelty, the way she said most things, and then she added, "There were like four hundred of us in ninth grade. You're going to find more than two."

His mother, watching from across the room, seemed to presage trouble whenever Mathis stood too long in one place with his jaw set like that, so she came over and asked him to help her carry the cake from the car. In the parking lot the evening light was still on the asphalt, and he told her, haltingly, that the list felt wrong now, that reading it would be like showing off the survivors.

"You don't have to read it," she said. "You could tell them the number instead."

"Which number?"

She unlocked the trunk and lifted the white box, letting him take the other side. "I looked it up for the newsletter at work. The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year." She balanced the cake on her hip, then let him take it entirely. "That's the official figure. Eighty-seven of every hundred finished."

Inside, the toasts had already begun. A boy named Deshawn, who was going to a state school on a running scholarship in the fall and wanted, more than anything, to be remembered at this dinner as the funniest person in the room, was halfway through an impression of their physics teacher. He had prepared three bits, and he was watching the tables the way a comedian watches for the laugh. When Mathis came back in with the cake, Deshawn seized the pause.

"Mathis has a speech," he announced. "I heard him saying so in the parking lot. Come on, big man. Verisimilitude. That's a word I learned for the SAT and I need to use it before I forget it, so give us something real."

Mathis set the cake down. He had intended a speech full of warm details, the time the fire alarm went off during the chemistry final, the teacher who called everyone "citizen." Standing there, he understood that the warm details and the missing faces were not two separate subjects, and that pretending otherwise would make the whole thing hollow. He took out the folded list but did not read the names.

"Four hundred and twelve of us started ninth grade together," he said. "Not all of them are here tonight, and I don't actually know all the reasons. Some moved, some left, some we just stopped noticing. I found out tonight that the US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. That's the whole country. I don't know what our school's number is, and honestly I'm not sure yet what the number means, whether it's mostly about the kids or mostly about everything around the kids. I have arguments with myself about it." He paused, and the room was quieter than he expected. "But I know I want to be somebody who does the counting, not somebody who only counts the people still in the room."

There was a scattered, uncertain applause, and then Priya stood up and said, "For the record, I think the number means both, and I have an essay about it that none of you are ever going to be assigned." That got the real laugh, and Deshawn got his, and the cake was cut and the room loosened into noise again.

Later, when the waiters were stacking chairs, Mathis found Deshawn by the door, checking his phone, scrolling through a video someone had already posted of Priya's line. "You got your laugh," Mathis said. "Was it enough?"

"It'll do till the next one," Deshawn said, pocketing the phone. He clapped Mathis on the shoulder and nodded toward the parking lot, where the last cars were pulling out one by one under the streetlights.

The banner over the left field fence had faded to the color of weak tea, and Victor had stopped seeing it weeks ago, the way you stop seeing anything that portends nothing good. It read REGIONALS 1998, the last year this town's team had gone anywhere, and it hung there like an affidavit swearing that nothing now happening on this diamond was worth the ink.

Victor was playing his one and only season, senior year, because his mother had said he would regret never trying and because Qasim had said, more persuasively, that the summer league needed a second baseman who could show up. He could show up. That turned out to matter more than anyone admitted.

The trouble arrived with Deely's bat. Deely, the shortstop, hit three doubles in one game in June, then two home runs the next night, and after that Qasim changed. Every relay, every called play, bent toward Deely. If Deely had reached base in his last at bat, Qasim fed him. If Deely had made an out, Qasim looked elsewhere, to Victor, to the gaps, to whoever the day had not yet disappointed.

"He's hot," Qasim said in the dugout against Millbrook, wiping sunflower shells off his thigh. "You ride the hot hand. Everybody knows that."

"Who's everybody?" Victor said.

"Everybody. My uncle. The guys on TV."

Victor let it go, because the season was short and Qasim's uncle was large and the score was 4-2. But that night, in his room, with a summer assignment on probability sitting half-finished on his desk, he typed a question into the search bar that he'd been carrying since the third double: do players actually get hot. He expected nothing. He found a study.

Three names, a year he made himself say aloud so it would stick. A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky. They had looked at basketball shooters, at the streaks everyone swore they saw, and concluded those streaks were no more common than chance. They called it the hot hand fallacy. Victor read the sentence four times. Then he read it again, slower, because it seemed to be saying that the thing happening in his infield every Tuesday and Thursday was a shared dream.

He did not tell Qasim right away. He was not sure why, except that Qasim had rigged his whole summer around the dream, and Victor had no replacement to offer, only subtraction. He tried it small, in the truck on the way to practice. "You know somebody studied this. Whether hot players stay hot."

"Studied what, hitting?"

"Shooting. Basketball. They found the streaks were just, like, what you'd get by chance anyway."

Qasim turned the volume knob up a click. "Different sport."

"Okay."

"Anyway you don't understand. You don't feel it. When you're hot, the ball looks big. It comes in slow."

"Maybe that's how it feels and still not how it is," Victor said, and Qasim pulled into the lot and cut the engine, which ended the conversation more efficiently than any argument could have.

The word fallacy he saved for the regional semifinal, which was generous of him, in retrospect. Tie game, seventh inning, Deely on second having doubled, and Qasim at the plate with Victor on third, one out, the infield in. The sign came down: safety squeeze, Victor breaks, Qasim protects. Except the sign came down twice, then a third time, and then the third base coach wiped it and put on the steal-and-read, which meant: Deely goes, and Qasim, if he can, hits where Deely is running.

"Same play as last week," Victor said at third, close to the coach's ear.

"Deely's on again. He hit the double."

"Coach, the streak isn't real. There was a study, they called it a fallacy. The guy who just hit two isn't more likely to hit a third."

The coach looked at Victor the way you look at a radar detector that has started speaking Latin. "The study studied basketball," he said, which was, Victor had to admit, what Qasim had said, and what he would probably say himself if some second baseman lectured him about probability in the seventh inning. Then the coach turned back to the field and repeated the sign.

Deely broke. The pitcher came set, and for one second Victor watched from third as the whole field bent toward Deely's streak, the catcher shifting, the shortstop cheating toward the bag, everyone obedient to a feeling that a dead professor in 1985 had measured and found empty. Qasim swung over the pitch. Deely was out by six feet.

They lost in the eighth, on a ground ball that skipped under Victor's glove with a runner on second, a ball he would tell himself for years he should have had. In the parking lot afterward, Qasim sat on the tailgate with his helmet still on. Victor stood a few feet off, not close enough to be comforting, not far enough to leave.

"Deely would've scored," Qasim said. "On a normal ground ball he scores."

"Maybe," Victor said. "The study doesn't say the guy won't hit. It just says you can't know."

Qasim pushed the helmet up with the heel of his hand. "Then what was the point of it?"

Victor looked back at the field, where the lights were still on over the empty diamond, the banner hanging obsolescent and stubborn in left. "I don't know," he said, and picked up the bag of balls by the fence.

Kaylee arrived at Mr. Ferreira's studio four minutes early, which was unusual, and sat down with the K. 545 score open on the music stand before he had finished arguing with his espresso machine. The argument was one-sided. The machine won, as it did every Tuesday, and he carried two small cups to the piano table anyway.

"You didn't have to bring me coffee," Kaylee said.

"I didn't. That one's mine. Yours is the one I'm pretending is yours." He set both cups down. "Today we stop playing and start reading. Mozart's C major sonata, first movement. I want you to find me the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation, and mark them in pencil."

She had prepared for playing, not for dissecting. At home she had listened to the movement twice with her eyes closed, then once with the score, and something had snagged: a new tune that arrived around the thirtieth bar, brighter somehow, like the music had changed rooms. She had circled it in pencil and written a question mark, and then, annoyed with herself, added a second question mark.

Mr. Ferreira's own want that afternoon was no secret; he was auditioning students for his spring recital in April, and he had told her mother, within Kaylee's hearing, that he wanted one of his teenagers to open the program with something clean and classical. He had been dropping hints for a month the way a cat drops a dead bird at the door.

"Where does the exposition end?" he asked now, pacing behind her chair.

"The repeat sign," she said. "Bar twenty-eight."

"And what happens inside it? Two themes. Where's the second one start?"

She put her finger on the bar with the question marks. "Here. Something new starts here. It sounds different."

"Different how?"

She had to be careful. She knew two things that didn't obviously fit together. Her theory textbook, which she read on the bus like a weirdo, had a sedimentary quality, layers of rules deposited over months, most of them half understood. One layer said that in a major-key movement in sonata form, the exposition's second theme is usually in the dominant key. The other thing she knew was what her ear told her, which was only that the tune felt brighter. She turned to the key signature and counted the F sharps.

"Wait," she said. "It's moved to G major."

"Which means what, if the movement started in C major?"

"That G is the dominant of C." She said it slowly, testing it the way you test ice. "So the second theme is in the dominant key. That's why it sounded brighter. It wasn't a mood, it was a key change."

"Mm." He drank his coffee, which was a form of applause.

She began to metabolize it, marking the score in pencil: exposition, with its first theme in C, its second in G; then the development, where the material got taken apart like an engine on a garage floor; then the recapitulation, where everything came back. She stopped at the recapitulation and frowned. The second theme came back, but the key signature had changed back, and when she played the passage, one-handed, the tune that had lived in G was now sitting in C.

"Both themes come home in the tonic," she said.

"Say it as a sentence and I'll believe you."

"In the recapitulation, the second theme comes back in C major instead of G." She looked up. "So the whole form is a shape. You leave home, you go to the dominant, and then you come back and everything's in the same key. It's an argument."

"It's a structure," he said. "Whether it's an argument depends on the player."

She thought about that while she penciled the final brackets. Her theory book wanted to make it a logos, a pure rational order you could state as a rule, and her ear kept insisting it was just a feeling of leaving and returning. Maybe it was both, and maybe the rule and the feeling were the same thing described twice. She couldn't decide, and she wrote a third question mark in the margin, small, for herself.

"April fourth," Mr. Ferreira said, very casually, collecting the cups. "The recital. K. 545, first movement. If you can play the development like you just analyzed it."

"The development is only thirty bars."

"The development is where you find out if the player has anything to say." He pointed at her score, at the bracket she had drawn around the section where everything breaks apart. "Play it like you know why it's breaking."

Kaylee closed the score, then opened it again to the first page, and set her hands on the piano.

Mathis had forty minutes before the library closed and one red bar standing between him and a working program. He had claimed the computer at the end of the row, the one beside the window where the evening light came in sideways across the keyboard, and next to a paperweight nobody needed in July, a fist of polished igneous rock that the librarians moved from desk to desk like a mascot.

The project had seemed simple when his cousin described it over the phone: build a class in Java with private fields, expose them through getter methods, then prove the whole thing worked with tests. Mathis had written the class in one sitting, a BankAccount with a private balance and a private owner name, a constructor, two getters. He had felt the satisfaction of it, the way the private keyword sealed the fields away like a door clicking shut. Then he had written the tests, and one of them refused to pass.

The failing message sat on his screen in unforgiving text. It told him the test expected one hundred and the balance was zero. He read it four times. He had deposited one hundred in the setup, or he thought he had, and no matter how many times he traced the lines with his finger, the deposit looked correct. He leaned back, and the chair's spring complained, and a girl two monitors down glanced over and then returned to her own screen, where rows of color-coded text scrolled like weather.

"You look like your code bit you," she said, not unkindly, without turning her head entirely.

"It's a test failure," Mathis said. "It says the expected value is one hundred, and the actual is zero. So my deposit isn't happening, except it is happening. I can see it happening."

She rolled her chair over, and he noticed the lanyard around her neck, a camp badge from the university two towns over. Her name, he learned later, was Priya. She read his test aloud, quietly, one line at a time, and then stopped at the assertion itself, where he had written the call that checks whether two values match.

"Wait," she said. "Which one is yours and which one is the program's?"

"What do you mean, which is mine?"

"Look at the order you put them in." She tapped the screen with a pen cap, twice, at the two numbers inside the parentheses. He had written the assertion with the program's balance first and the number one hundred second. In his head the order had felt natural, his result, then what it should be, the way you'd say "I got ninety but I expected a hundred." He waited for her to tell him the fix, but she only shrugged and said, "Try switching them and see what the message says."

He swapped the two values and ran the test again. The red bar stayed red, but the message had changed its posture entirely. Now it read that the test expected zero and the actual value was one hundred, and Mathis sat very still, because the message was telling the truth about his code but from the wrong side of the glass. "The expected value comes first," he said slowly, "and the actual second. I had them backward. The message wasn't lying. It was just describing my deposit as the dream and zero as the reality."

"So your deposit works," Priya said.

"My deposit works." The remaining red bar had to be a different problem, and it was: he found it within a minute, a getter returning the owner's name when the test asked for the balance, a copy-paste wound he closed the way you'd suture a small cut, one careful line rejoining what belonged together. He ran the full suite. Green. All green. He let out a breath that made the igneous paperweight's neighbor, a plant with skeptical leaves, shiver slightly.

Priya was already back at her own machine, but she turned once more. "Where'd you get the skeleton, the empty class you started from?" she asked.

And here was the thing Mathis had not told anyone, not his cousin, not the friend who had asked to see his project. The empty class had not been his. He had found it in a repository online late one night, fields declared, methods stubbed, waiting like scaffolding around a house someone else had framed. He had assumed that starting from someone else's bones didn't count, that only the filling-in counted, but sitting here with the tests passing, he understood the question mattered. The provenance of the code was part of the code.

"My cousin sent me a template," he said, which was true in the way a half-truth is true, and then, because the green bar had made him briefly brave, he added, "and I found part of it online. A starting point. I'm going to rewrite it from scratch tonight so it's all mine."

"From scratch," Priya repeated, as if testing the phrase, and rolled back to her screen.

The overhead announcement came, ten minutes to closing. Mathis saved his work, then opened a blank file and typed the first line of the class, public class BankAccount, and this time no one had written it before him. He typed the private fields himself, balance and owner, and outside the window a streetlamp came on, humming, as he wrote the first getter, one hand shading the screen from the glare.

"Expected first," he murmured to the empty chair beside him, and ran the test.

The library had kept its back tables for the math club on Thursday afternoons all year, and by late May the librarians had stopped coming over except to shush the table nearest the periodicals. Keira spread her notebook flat, weighted the curling corner with a pencil case, and copied the problem Theo had written on the whiteboard they wheeled in from the storage closet. Between the line and the parabola, find the area enclosed where they cross. She had until Saturday to be fluent in this, because the regional exam offered a scholarship, and the scholarship, if she got it, would decide whether she took the dorms or the bus.

Theo worked fast, head down, the way he always did when he wanted to be the first to call out an answer. Across the table Nadia was slower, checking her intersections twice, and Keira liked watching her work, the small nods she gave herself when a line of algebra came out clean. Their faculty advisor was at a conference, which meant the club ran on its own steam, and today that meant a wager: whoever got the area first got the last of the pizza that the disbursement from the student council had paid for, a reimbursement Theo had chased for three weeks and now guarded like a treasury.

"Four thirds," Theo said, twelve minutes in, and turned his paper so they could see it.

Nadia looked up, then down at her own page. "I got four thirds too, but negative. Negative four thirds."

"You subtracted wrong," Theo said. "Backwards."

"No, you did." She said it without heat, the way she disputed things, as though the question were genuinely open. She slid her paper across, and Keira leaned in. Both of them had found the same crossing points, the same interval, the same antiderivative. The only difference was the order of the subtraction inside the integral: Theo had written the parabola first, Nadia had written the line first, and the two answers were opposites.

Keira put her finger on the two papers, side by side. She had an inchoate sense of what was wrong, a feeling like reaching for a light switch in an unfamiliar room, and she did not trust it yet, so she went back to the picture. She drew the two curves roughly, freehand, in the margin of her notebook, and shaded between them with the side of her pencil. The shaded region sat under one curve and above the other; that was what "between" meant, she could see it now that she had drawn it instead of only pushing symbols around. On the interval where they'd integrated, the line was the upper curve and the parabola the lower one, all the way across.

"You have to subtract the upper function minus the lower one," she said, mostly to the paper. "Over the interval where they're ordered that way."

Nadia tilted her head. "Then mine's backwards."

"Then yours is backwards," Keira said, and felt the switch click on. It wasn't that the symbol method had failed; it was that the symbols were answering a question only the picture could ask. Her calculus teacher all year had pushed the algebra, drill after drill, and Keira had imputed her own slowness to some missing rigor, when what she'd been missing was the drawing. She had treated the picture as decoration. It was the specification.

Theo had already flipped his paper over and redone the subtraction in the correct order, and when his answer came out four thirds, positive, he tapped the pencil against the table twice. "Same number," he said. "I was right for no reason. That's worse."

"It is worse," Nadia said, and pulled the pizza box toward herself. "You get no pizza for right answers with no defense." She lifted the last slice out and held it over the box, considering, then broke it along the middle and set half on a napkin in front of Keira. "For the picture," Nadia said. "The picture is what decided it."

Keira ate the half slice slowly and redrew her diagram once more, cleanly this time, the line above, the parabola below, the strip between them shaded in careful parallel strokes. She wrote under it, in small letters, upper minus lower, where they're ordered that way, and boxed the words. On Saturday she would have to be fast, and she was not fast yet. But she understood something she could rebuild from nothing if the formula slipped away, and she sat with that a moment, the window light going long across the table, the whiteboard waiting to be erased.

"Next one," Theo said, and turned the board around, and Keira picked up her pencil.

Juliette arrived at Mrs. Okafor's studio with the K. 310 score flat under her arm like a shield, because she had promised, twice, that this week she would finally mark the exposition, development and recapitulation in pencil instead of just humming along and hoping the form would confess on its own. The studio smelled of rosin and the lemon polish Mrs. Okafor applied to the piano bench with the devotion other people gave to prayer. Dev was already there, sprawled on the window seat with his own copy of the same Andante cantabile, and he saluted her with his pencil, which was, Juliette noted, entirely unsharpened.

"You've marked nothing," she said.

"I've marked a system of belief," Dev said. "The development starts where the music stops being polite. The recapitulation starts where it apologizes."

"That's not analysis, that's a horoscope."

Mrs. Okafor, who had been watering a doomed fern near the radiator, said without turning around, "Pencils, both of you. Brackets. Measure numbers. I want to see evidence, not vibes." She sat down at the piano, and Juliette opened her score on the rack with the grim ceremony of someone submitting to a trial she intended to win. She had spent Sunday evening with the recording, listening three times through, and she had drawn a firm double bar and a triumphant arrow at the place where the opening theme came back. She was proud of that arrow. She had even decorated it, which she now regretted.

She played her marks like a case for the prosecution. "Exposition, first theme, second theme in the dominant, fine, that part everyone agrees on. Development begins here. And the recapitulation is here, obviously, because the first tune comes back right here, listen." She reached over and played the passage herself, the opening theme, unmistakable, and Dev leaned forward on the window seat as if pulled by the collar.

"It's back," he said.

"It's back," Juliette agreed, with the modesty of someone expecting an acquittal.

Mrs. Okafor played the same eight measures and then kept going, and Juliette's ears, which had begun to acclimate to the movement's grammar across three evenings, noticed something they had glided over before: underneath the familiar tune, the harmony was not home. It was the dominant chord, the home key's dominant, churning and holding, and the music underneath was not resting, it was coiling. The tune floated above it like a face leaning out a window while the house kept moving. And then the passage ended, and the theme dissolved, and it was not the recapitulation at all, and Juliette sat very still with her decorated arrow suddenly incriminating her.

"That's the retransition," Dev said quietly, pointing at the spot, and she remembered him mentioning it once, weeks ago, in the hallway, when she had been too busy to listen.

"So it teases you," Juliette said. "Near the end of the development, it just sits on the dominant and dangles the first theme in front of you, and you lean forward because you think it's about to come home, and it isn't. Not yet." She erased the arrow, which left a small gray ghost on the page, a shadow of her former confidence. The pugnacious little opening motive, the one that had swaggered in at measure one, turned out to be a mimic as well, willing to impersonate its own return.

"The question," Mrs. Okafor said, "is whether Mozart is lying to you or telling you a truth you're not ready for. You may take either position. You may not take both at once and call it a grade."

Juliette flipped through her notes from Sunday, where she had written things like "hopeful!!" and "finally calm" in the margins like a diary, and she saw now that she had documented her own deception in real time. She drew the true recapitulation bracket twenty-two measures later than her arrow, at the moment the harmony actually landed on the tonic and the theme arrived with its feet on the ground, and beside the earlier passage she wrote, in small letters, "false alarm, enjoy it anyway." Dev leaned over to read it.

"That's not scholarly notation," he said.

"It's my considered position," Juliette said. "The tease is part of the piece. Whether Mozart means it kindly or not, I genuinely can't tell you, and I refuse to pretend." She wrote one more thing in the margin, held it up so Dev could see, and tapped it twice with her pencil, which was, unlike his, sharp.

The textbook had been open on the tailgate of the pickup for forty minutes, and Hudson still could not make the page mean anything. Glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, energy. His uncle's farm smelled of cut hay and diesel, and the words on the page smelled of nothing at all. He was supposed to trace it, the teacher had said. Glucose to ATP, step by step, in the mitochondria, and if he failed the retake on Thursday he would lose his spot on the cross-country team for the season. That was the rule: no D's, no races.

"You're staring at that thing like it bit you," his cousin Marisol said, lugging a bucket of water past the truck. She was fourteen and enjoyed his suffering the way younger cousins enjoy most things, openly and without shame.

"It's cellular respiration. It's due tomorrow. I don't get it."

"Then get the cows to do it for you." She set the bucket down in front of the fence, and the animals came, unhurried, their breath steaming in the cold. Hudson watched them drink, and then he watched them breathe, and something in his head tilted sideways but did not yet fall.

He walked out to the pond behind the lower pasture because he could not sit still, which was the whole reason he ran in the first place. The pond had a skin of green algae at the shallows, and a film of ice beginning at the reeds. He stood there with the book under his arm and breathed out, a long plume of white, and thought about what he was actually exhaling. Carbon dioxide. Six molecules of it, if the equation was true, for every glucose. C6H12O6 plus six O2, going in. Six CO2 and six H2O, plus energy, coming out. He said it aloud to the pond, which absorbed it without comment. The carbon in his breath had been carbon in a sugar, which had been carbon in the bread he ate at breakfast, which had been, before that, carbon in a plant somewhere. The thought was either beautiful or a kind of vertigo. He could not decide.

His phone buzzed. A message from his lab partner, Denis, who had failed the same test: "i figured out the trick. you breathe on the equation. literally. glucose + 6 O2 becomes 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy. everything on the left is what goes in, everything on the right is what you breathe out and pee out and run on. mitochondria are the factory. also do you have my pencil."

Hudson typed back, "your pencil is in your hair," and then stood there holding the phone because Denis was right about the equation and probably wrong about the pencil, and both of these felt like ordinary facts of the universe. He exhaled again at the pond. There. That cloud was six CO2's worth, or near enough, and somewhere inside his cells the mitochondria were doing the whole transaction right now, paying him in ATP so he could stand here thinking about it. Running was just spending that currency faster. Thursday's race, if he kept his eligibility, would be the equation performed at speed.

He went back to the barn, where Marisol was throwing hay down from the loft and being theatrical about her arms. "I figured it out," he said.

"Congratulations. Do you know where the carbon in your breath came from?"

She said it to mock him, but it was the exact question, so he took it seriously, which annoyed her. "Sugar I ate. The equation turns glucose and oxygen into carbon dioxide and water and energy. Six of each coming out. The carbon goes from the sugar to the breath."

"That's the most boring magic trick I've ever heard."

"It's not a trick. It's accounting." And that, he realized, was the position he had been circling all afternoon without landing on. His teacher wanted him to see respiration as an elegant cascade, enzymes and electrons, a cathedral of chemistry. Denis wanted him to see it as a ledger, inputs and outputs, a machine you could breathe on to test. Hudson had been trying to choose between them, and standing in the barn with the hay dust turning in the light, he understood he did not have to. It was both, and the cathedral view was why the thing was beautiful, and the ledger view was why he would pass the retake. What stayed uncertain, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it, was why sugar becoming breath felt like anything at all, why atoms rearranging themselves in his mitochondria added up to a boy who wanted to run on Thursday. He could write the equation on the test and still not know that. Solipsism, the philosophy elective had taught him, was the belief that only your own mind is real, and sometimes, tracing carbon from a wheat field through his own blood and out into the cold air, he felt the opposite danger: that he was nothing but carbon, rearranged, and that this was somehow fine.

Marisol's phone, propped on a post, was playing some influencer telling her that breathing exercises could "flush toxins," and she was nodding along. Hudson told her, with some satisfaction, that this was pernicious nonsense, that breathing out was carbon dioxide and water, not toxins, and that if she wanted to flush something she should drink actual water. She threw a fistful of hay at his head. He ducked, and it drifted past him into the shaft of light from the loft door, each strand falling slow, the way snow would fall later that night, while he sat at the kitchen table with the book open and a pencil, writing the equation out one more time, left to right, then breathing on the glass of the window to watch it fog.

Kevin had signed up for Advanced Studio because the college application asked for something that looked like commitment, and because his mother had said, once, that his grandfather painted. He had no evidence of this beyond a watercolor of a savanna that hung in the hallway of her apartment, dull yellows gone brown at the edges, and he had begun, without quite deciding to, a copy of it. The copy was going badly.

The problem was the gray. He had mixed a gray for the distant thunderclouds, the same gray in the same pan, and painted a single long bank of it across the top of his canvas. On the left side, where it sat above the yellowed grass, the gray looked warm, almost rosy. On the right, above a patch of blue sky he had laid in earlier, it went cold and flat, like slate. He leaned back and looked at it for a long time, chin resting on the handle of a brush he was not using.

At the next table, Priya was arguing with her own canvas, a portrait of her brother that she claimed looked like a stranger. Kevin had never spoken to her before the second week of class, and now they spoke constantly, mostly in complaints. He carried his canvas over and set it on her table. "Same paint," he said. "One gray. Tell me it doesn't look like two."

Priya looked. She looked for longer than politeness required, her thumbprint of green still drying on her cheek where she had scratched it. "It looks like two," she said. "That's disgusting. How did you do that?"

"I didn't do anything. It's the same tube."

He spent that evening not painting but searching on his phone in the kitchen while his mother made rice, and the search kept turning up the same thing from different directions. A chemist, Michel Eugène Chevreul, had published something in 1839 called the law of simultaneous contrast. It described how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. He read the sentence three times. Complement: the color opposite on the wheel, blue against orange, yellow against violet. His gray wasn't two grays. It was one gray being pushed around by its neighbors, pulled warm by the yellow grass, pulled cold by the blue sky. He felt the specific pleasure of a thing snapping into place, and then, immediately, the suspicion that he had it wrong, that he had found a fact the way you find a coin on the sidewalk and assumed the whole street was paved with them.

The next afternoon he tested it, because Priya, wiping her hands on her apron, said, "You should just paint a stripe of it on white and see." He did. He painted three identical stripes of the gray on white, on orange, on blue, and propped the board against the window ledge where everyone in the class walked past it. Nobody commented except Marcus, who said, "Is that a project?" and Kevin said, "Sort of," which was not a lie. The stripes shifted. On the orange ground the gray leaned blue; on the blue ground it leaned orange. Same paint, same brush, three different grays.

He sat with that for a while, brush balanced across his water jar. He could pretend he hadn't seen it and repaint the sky the way the reference wanted, forcing the thundercloud to be neutral, a gray that was gray all the way across. Or he could let the painting be two grays, warm over the grass and cold over the sky, and call it intentional. He thought about his grandfather, who had painted the savanna with grass so yellow it was nearly orange, and whether the old man had known any of this or had simply pushed paint around until something looked right. There was no way to ask. There was no way to know whether the watercolor was accurate or invented, whether the clouds had actually looked warm.

In the end he did neither thing cleanly. He dulled the blue of the sky a little, and warmed the gray slightly with a thread of raw sienna, and let the remaining difference stand, because it was truer to what a storm over yellow grass would do, and because a painting that admitted its own trickery seemed more honest than one that hid it. He was not certain this was right. He was certain only that the gray behaved the way it behaved, indifferent to what he wanted, and that his job was to work with it rather than over it.

Priya came over at the end of class, still wearing the green on her cheek. She looked at the clouds, then at the stripe board, still propped by the window. "So it's real," she said.

"It's real," Kevin said. "A chemist figured it out in 1839, and I got it wrong for two weeks." He turned the canvas toward the light, and the two grays sat there, quietly not matching.

The sticky notes had cost Thomas an hour he did not have. One yellow, one blue, one green, trimmed to fit the margins of the miniature score of Mozart's K. 333, and each one drifting out of position every time he opened the programme booklet to check them again. He was in row J of the Marshall Concert Hall, twenty minutes early, because the exam on Tuesday would ask him to mark the form of this very movement, and his teacher had said, with what Thomas considered unnecessary cheer, that hearing it live would fix it in his mind better than any recording.

Beside him, a woman was reading a thick paperback with a cover he recognised from his mother's shelf, something about immunology, its margins dense with pencil. When the house lights dimmed she tucked it away, and Thomas felt obscurely reassured, as though the presence of a stranger who studied one difficult thing made his own studying legitimate.

The first movement began, and Thomas followed with his finger in the score. He had marked the blue note at bar one, where the first theme arrived, all descending softness, and then, at the double bar, the yellow note for the development. That was the plan. Exposition, then the part where Mozart picked the themes up and carried them through other keys, then, at the green note near the end, the recapitulation, when the themes came home. His teacher had drawn the three words on the board once and refused to elaborate; the class had been left, querulous and muttering, to codify the whole system for themselves.

The trouble arrived in the development. Somewhere in the middle of it, Thomas lost his place. The pianist took a passage at a speed the recording he practised with never approached, and the themes blurred into one another, and when Thomas found the line again the music was doing something so tender and strange that he forgot the notes entirely. He sat with his finger pressed against a bar he could not name. Was this still the working-through, or had the return already begun without him?

He glanced sideways. The woman with the immunology book was listening with her eyes shut, and something in her stillness made him feel both foolish and braver. He could not rewind the hall. He had one chance at this, the way she presumably had one chance at an experiment that would not repeat itself.

Then the first theme came back, and Thomas's stomach dropped, because it came back and it was wrong. The shape was unmistakable, the same descending figure, but the key beneath it had shifted, darker than before, not home at all. He looked at his green sticky note, which he had placed with such confidence on Sunday night, and understood that he had put it in the wrong place. The themes had returned before the true return, Mozart letting him hear them in a stranger's country first, and only later, after a small hinge of transition he would never have noticed in the recording, did the same figure settle back into the original key, and the green note should have gone there. He moved it. His hands were almost steady.

Afterwards, in the lobby with its marble and its surge of coats, he found Nadia by the doors. "Did you get the recapitulation?" she asked, gripping her own battered score. "I had it four bars late."

"Twelve," Thomas said. "The theme came back early and I believed it." He showed her the green note in its new position, its edge already losing its stick. "The real one brings it back in the same key. Everything before that is still the development, still travelling."

"So we both got it wrong."

"We both got it wrong twice, and then right once," Thomas said. The woman from row J passed them on her way out, the immunology book under her arm, and she caught the word recapitulation as she went and smiled at them both, briefly, like a signal between people who mark things and move them.

"Tuesday, then," Nadia said, and pushed open the heavy door into the cold.
